Sensitive communication (an angry or upset patient)
CSE: the prescribing guidance, drug chart, TTO and syringe driver
A colleague's error, and raising a concern
Visual fields, eye movements and pupils
CSE: notes on a post-take ward round (Paper B, alternative)
CSE: prescribing on a drug chart (Paper C)

CSE: a referral letter from GP notes

The patient not taking their medication

abcde.summary: Any deteriorating patient: assess and treat as you go, **A to E**, call for help early and reassess after every intervention. Examiners mark the order, and that you act on each problem before moving on.

sections.title: Start
items: Check the area is safe; introduce yourself; ask “How are you?” — a normal reply means the airway is patent, they are breathing and perfusing their brain
**Call for help early** (senior; 2222 if peri-arrest). Ask for obs, monitoring and IV access

sections.title: A — Airway
items: Look, listen, feel: talking? stridor, gurgling, snoring, see-saw breathing
Open it: head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust, suction, adjuncts. An airway at risk = anaesthetist now
Critically ill: **15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask**, then titrate to 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of CO₂ retention)

sections.title: B — Breathing
items: Respiratory rate, SpO₂, work of breathing, trachea, expansion, percussion, auscultation
ABG; portable chest X-ray
Treat what you find: nebulised salbutamol for bronchospasm, needle decompression for a tension pneumothorax

sections.title: C — Circulation
items: Pulse, BP, capillary refill, colour and temperature of the skin, JVP, heart sounds, urine output
**Two large-bore cannulae** (grey/green): FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, clotting, group and save/crossmatch, blood cultures, lactate, VBG
Fluid challenge: **500 mL crystalloid over <15 min**, then reassess (smaller, e.g. 250 mL, if heart failure is a worry)
12-lead ECG; catheter for hourly urine output if shocked

sections.title: D — Disability
items: AVPU or GCS; pupils; **capillary glucose** (treat <4 mmol/L)
Drug chart: opioids or sedatives (naloxone for opioid toxicity); seizures, focal signs, neck stiffness

sections.title: E — Exposure
items: Expose fully, with dignity: rashes (non-blanching?), bleeding, wounds, drains, calves, abdomen; temperature
Review the charts, notes and recent results

sections.title: Then
items: Reassess from A after any intervention or change
Escalate with **SBAR**; give a working diagnosis and the ceiling of care
Sepsis: the **Sepsis Six** within the hour — oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output (UK Sepsis Trust)

pairs.title: Numbers that decide what you do
rows: Emergency response; consider critical care (RCP NEWS2)
Lactate ≥4 mmol/L or systolic BP <90 in suspected sepsis
High risk: IV antibiotics within 1 hour, fluid bolus, senior review (NICE NG51)
IM adrenaline 1:1000 **0.5 mg (0.5 mL)** adult, anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 min if no better (RCUK 2021)
IV 10% glucose or IM glucagon 1 mg (JBDS)

tips: Treat as you find: don't move on from A with an obstructed airway.
Say “I would call for senior help now” early — it scores, and it's right.
Reassess after every intervention, out loud.
The usual scenarios: sepsis, anaphylaxis, acute asthma, hypoglycaemia, GI bleed, opioid toxicity, PE.

cxr.summary: Check the film, then a fixed ABCDE read. Describe what you see before naming it, and end with what you'd do.

sections.title: The film
items: Patient details, date; PA or AP; **RIPE**: rotation, inspiration (5–6 anterior ribs), projection, exposure

sections.title: ABCDE
items: **A**irway: trachea central?
**B**reathing: lung fields zone by zone, pleura, costophrenic angles
**C**ardiac: size (CTR <0.5 on a PA film), borders
**D**iaphragm: free air underneath?
**E**verything else: bones, soft tissue, lines and tubes

pairs.title: Patterns
rows: Visible lung edge, no markings beyond
Veil-like left upper zone; sail sign behind the heart
Left upper / left lower lobe collapse
Alveolar oedema, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, effusions

tips: Say RIPE out loud.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: don't wait for the film.

low-mood-hx.summary: Assess the core and biological symptoms of depression, screen the differentials (bipolar, organic, substance) and — critically — perform a risk assessment.

sections.title: Core symptoms (≥2 weeks)
items: Low mood, **anhedonia** (loss of interest/pleasure), low energy/fatigue

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Suicide**: Have you felt life isn't worth living? Thought of ending it? Any plans or preparations? What stops you?
**Risk to others and safeguarding**: Are there children at home, or anyone who depends on you? Any thoughts of harming someone else?
**Psychosis**: Hearing or seeing things others don't? Feeling watched or controlled?
**Bipolar (changes the treatment)**: Ever had spells of feeling high, full of energy, needing little sleep?
**Self-neglect**: Are you eating, drinking, looking after yourself?

sections.title: Biological & cognitive
items: Sleep (early-morning waking), appetite/weight, concentration, libido, diurnal variation
Guilt, worthlessness, hopelessness

sections.title: Risk assessment (never skip)
items: Thoughts of self-harm or suicide — **ideation → plan → intent → means**; protective factors
Risk to others; risk from others; self-neglect

sections.title: Screen differentials
items: **Manic/hypomanic** episodes ever (bipolar), psychotic symptoms, alcohol/substance use, thyroid symptoms, medications, recent stressors

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Postnatal depression** (came up 2023): onset within the year after birth; ask about bonding, feeding and sleep beyond the baby's, and **thoughts of harming herself or the baby**. Baby blues (days 3 to 10, settles within 2 weeks) is not depression; confusion, hallucinations or delusions in the first weeks = **postpartum psychosis**, a psychiatric emergency (NICE CG192)

**Anxiety, or a psychiatric history from scratch** (came up 2025): presenting complaint, then past psychiatric history, forensic history, substances, personal history, premorbid personality, and the risk assessment every time

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Low mood + anhedonia + biological symptoms ≥2 weeks

tips: **Always do the risk assessment** — asking about suicide does not increase risk and can fail the station if omitted.
Screen for a manic episode — it changes the diagnosis to bipolar and the treatment.
Anhedonia is the most discriminating core symptom.

gi-hx.summary: Location + character + associated GI/urinary/gynae symptoms localise the cause. Always consider the surgical abdomen and, in women, an ectopic pregnancy.

sections.title: Characterise (SOCRATES)
items: Site (which quadrant), onset, character (colicky vs constant), radiation (loin-to-groin, to back, to shoulder tip), timing, relation to food/movement, severity

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **AAA**: Pain through to the back? Did you collapse or faint? A pulsing in the tummy? Over 65, a smoker, a known aneurysm?
**Ectopic pregnancy**: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period? Bleeding, pain on one side, shoulder-tip pain, feeling faint? A previous ectopic, PID or a coil?
**Perforation or peritonitis**: Worse on moving or coughing, so you lie still?
**Bowel obstruction**: Vomiting? Have your bowels or wind stopped? Swollen tummy, colicky pain? Previous surgery or a hernia?
**Upper GI bleed**: Vomited blood or coffee grounds? Black, tarry stools? On NSAIDs, steroids or blood thinners? Alcohol or liver disease?
**Mesenteric ischaemia**: Pain far worse than it looks, after meals? An irregular heartbeat (AF)?

sections.title: Associated symptoms
items: GI: nausea/vomiting, bowel habit change, blood/melaena, appetite/weight
Urinary: dysuria, frequency, haematuria
Gynae: LMP, discharge, pregnancy possibility (β-hCG)
Systemic: fever, jaundice

sections.title: By location
items: RUQ: biliary (Murphy’s), hepatitis
Epigastric: peptic ulcer, pancreatitis (radiates to back), MI
RIF: appendicitis, ectopic, ovarian
Loin-to-groin colic: renal stone
Central→RIF migrating: appendicitis

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Central pain migrating to RIF, anorexia, low-grade fever
RUQ pain after fatty food, Murphy’s positive if inflamed
Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, alcohol/gallstones
Loin-to-groin colicky pain, haematuria, can’t lie still
Female, missed period, PV bleeding, positive β-hCG — exclude in every woman

tips: Do a pregnancy test in **every** woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain.
Migratory central-to-RIF pain with anorexia is classic appendicitis.
Consider a leaking AAA in any older patient with abdominal/back pain and collapse.

sexual-hx.summary: Private, confidential, non-judgemental — “I ask everyone these questions”. Symptoms, the last sexual contact and partners, protection, previous STIs and testing, contraception, and safeguarding.

sections.title: Set up
items: Privacy; explain confidentiality and its limits; normalise the questions

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Safeguarding and exploitation**: How old are your partners? Under 16? Ever felt pressured, or had sex you didn't want?
**Ectopic pregnancy**: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period? Bleeding, pain on one side, shoulder-tip pain, feeling faint? A previous ectopic, PID or a coil?
**PEP window**: Any unprotected sex in the last 72 hours?
**PID**: Pelvic pain, fever, pain during sex?
**HIV seroconversion**: A flu-like illness or rash a few weeks after a risk?

sections.title: Symptoms
items: Discharge, dysuria, ulcers, lumps, rash, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, testicular pain, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding

sections.title: Partners
items: Last sexual intercourse; partner's gender; regular or casual; number in the last 3 months
Type of sex (oral, vaginal, anal); condom use; partner's symptoms; partner from a high-prevalence country

sections.title: Background
items: Previous STIs; HIV and hepatitis tests; vaccines (HPV, hepatitis B); contraception, LMP
Risks: sex work, MSM, injecting drug use, chemsex

sections.title: Safeguarding
items: Under 16: Fraser guidelines and Gillick competence; age gap, coercion, exploitation

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **HIV seroconversion** (came up 2025, as a sore throat after a fever): 2 to 6 weeks after exposure, a flu-like illness: **fever, sore throat, rash, swollen glands**, mouth ulcers. Take the exposure history (partners, condoms, PrEP, needles), test with a 4th-generation HIV test, and PEP if the exposure was within 72 hours (BASHH)

tips: Explain window periods when testing.
Partner notification is part of the plan.

paeds-hx.summary: From a parent: the presenting complaint, then the paediatric frame — birth, feeding, growth, development, immunisations — and the social picture, with safeguarding in mind.

sections.title: The frame
items: Birth: gestation, delivery, birth weight, any neonatal unit stay
Feeding: breast or bottle, volumes, weaning; wet nappies (about 6 a day)
Growth (the red book), development across the four domains, immunisations
Past illnesses, medicines, allergies; family history (consanguinity)

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Sepsis or meningitis**: Fever, floppy or hard to wake, a rash that doesn't fade under a glass, not feeding?
**Dehydration**: How many wet nappies today? Drinking? Sunken eyes, no tears?
**Bilious vomiting (malrotation)**: Is the vomit green?
**Developmental regression**: Has your child lost any skills they used to have?
**Safeguarding**: Who looks after them? Any injuries, and how did they happen? Any delay in coming?

sections.title: Social
items: Who lives at home, nursery or school, smoking at home, social worker involvement

sections.title: Adolescents
items: See them alone for part of it: HEADSSS (home, education, activities, drugs, sex, suicide/mood, safety)

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Febrile convulsion** (came up often, last 2024): the seizure itself (what it looked like, how long, one side or both, how long to recover), the fever and its source, meningitis signs, vaccinations, family history. **Simple**: 6 months to 5 years, generalised, under 15 minutes, once in the illness, fully recovered within an hour; **complex** if focal, longer, recurrent or slow to recover (NICE CKS). Then counsel: common, usually harmless, what to do next time, when to call 999

**Crying or vomiting baby** (came up repeatedly): feeding (amount, frequency, technique), the vomit (**green = bilious = obstruction**; projectile at 2 to 8 weeks = pyloric stenosis), stools, wet nappies, weight on the red book, fever, and how the parent is coping
**ADHD or autism, from a parent** (came up 2023): what worries them, since when (before 12 for ADHD), at home and at school (reports from both), development, sleep, family history; their support

**Abdominal pain, collateral from a parent** (came up 2025): where, how long, vomiting, bowels (constipation is common), urine, fever, school and home (stress, bullying, safeguarding); see an older child alone (HEADSSS)

redflags: Delay in presenting, a story that doesn't fit the injury, a changing story — safeguarding
tips: Thank the parent and use the child's name.
Ask what the parent is most worried about.

cvs-exam.summary: A focused precordial exam — inspect, palpate, auscultate the four valve areas, then look for heart failure. The commonest OSCE examination; a slick routine scores across every domain.

sections.title: General inspection
items: End of the bed: comfortable at rest? breathless, cyanosed, cachectic?
Around the bed: GTN spray, oxygen, fluid restriction sign, medications, mobility aids

sections.title: Hands
items: Inspect: clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler’s nodes (endocarditis), tar staining, peripheral cyanosis, tendon xanthomata
Temperature; capillary refill (<2 s)
Radial pulse — rate & rhythm; **radio-radial delay** (coarctation/subclavian stenosis)
Offer to check for a **collapsing pulse** (aortic regurgitation)
Blood pressure (state you would measure it; wide pulse pressure = AR, narrow = AS)

sections.title: Face & neck
items: Eyes: conjunctival pallor (anaemia), corneal arcus, xanthelasma
Mouth: central cyanosis, high-arched palate (Marfan), dental hygiene (endocarditis risk)
Assess the **JVP** (raised in right heart failure/fluid overload); hepatojugular reflux
Palpate the **carotid** pulse — character (slow-rising = AS, collapsing = AR)

sections.title: Praecordium — inspect
items: Scars: median sternotomy, left thoracotomy, pacemaker or ICD
Visible pulsations, chest deformity

sections.title: Praecordium — palpate
items: Apex beat — normally 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (displaced in cardiomegaly; heaving = pressure overload, thrusting = volume)
Heaves (left parasternal = RV hypertrophy) and thrills (palpable murmur)

sections.title: Praecordium — auscultate
items: Four areas — **A**ortic (2nd R ICS), **P**ulmonary (2nd L ICS), **T**ricuspid (4th L ICS), **M**itral (5th ICS MCL) — “**APTM**”
Time each murmur against the carotid pulse (systolic vs diastolic)
Accentuate: **mitral** — left lateral, bell, expiration; **aortic** — sitting forward, expiration
Auscultate the carotids for radiation/bruits, and lung bases for crepitations

sections.title: Legs
items: Ankle and sacral oedema
Saphenous vein harvest scars (CABG)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Ejection-systolic murmur radiating to carotids + slow-rising pulse
Early-diastolic murmur (sitting forward) + collapsing pulse + wide pulse pressure
Mid-diastolic rumble, loud S1, tapping apex (left lateral)
Splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler’s nodes, new murmur
Raised JVP, peripheral oedema, bibasal crepitations

tips: Time murmurs against the **carotid**, not the radial (radial lags).
Know the two accentuation manoeuvres (left lateral for mitral, sitting forward for aortic).
Always comment on the JVP — commonly forgotten.

bbn.summary: Use the **SPIKES** framework: deliver serious news honestly, at the patient’s pace, responding to emotion. The single most tested comms scenario.

sections.title: S — Setting
items: Private room, sit down, no interruptions (bleep away), offer a chaperone/relative
Introduce yourself, confirm identity, check who they’d like present

sections.title: P — Perception
items: Find out what they already know and understand — “What have you been told so far?”

sections.title: I — Invitation
items: Ask how much they want to know — “Are you the kind of person who likes all the details?”

sections.title: K — Knowledge
items: Fire a **warning shot** — “I’m afraid I have some difficult news.”
Give information in small chunks, plain language, then pause
Avoid jargon and euphemisms; be honest and clear

sections.title: E — Emotions
items: Respond to the emotion — “I can see this is a shock.” Allow **silence**; offer tissues
Acknowledge and validate; don’t rush to reassure

sections.title: S — Strategy & summary
items: Give a clear plan and next steps; check understanding
Offer written information, support and a point of contact; safety-net; arrange follow-up

pitfalls: Filling the silence too quickly with facts or false reassurance.
Using euphemisms (“growth”, “passed away”) that obscure the message.
Overloading with a monologue instead of chunking and checking.
Forgetting to arrange follow-up and support.

resp-exam.summary: Inspect → palpate → percuss → auscultate the chest front and back, comparing sides. The pattern of findings localises the pathology (consolidation vs effusion vs pneumothorax vs fibrosis).

sections.title: General inspection
items: At rest: respiratory rate, work of breathing, accessory muscles, pursed lips, audible wheeze/stridor
Around the bed: oxygen, inhalers, nebuliser, sputum pot, cigarettes

sections.title: Hands
items: Clubbing (fibrosis, bronchiectasis, cancer), tar staining, peripheral cyanosis
Fine tremor (β-agonist), **CO₂ retention flap** (asterixis), bounding pulse (CO₂ retention)
Respiratory rate (count discreetly)

sections.title: Face & neck
items: Eyes: conjunctival pallor, Horner’s (apical/Pancoast tumour)
Mouth: central cyanosis
Trachea — central or deviated (**towards** collapse/fibrosis, **away** from large effusion/tension pneumothorax)
Cricosternal distance (hyperexpansion in COPD); lymphadenopathy

sections.title: Chest — inspect & palpate
items: Scars, deformity (barrel chest, kyphoscoliosis), asymmetry
Chest expansion — reduced on the side of pathology
Tactile vocal fremitus — increased over consolidation, decreased over effusion/pneumothorax

sections.title: Chest — percuss & auscultate
items: Percussion: **dull** = consolidation/collapse; **stony dull** = effusion; **hyper-resonant** = pneumothorax/COPD
Auscultate breath sounds + added sounds; compare sides, front and back
Vocal resonance to confirm the percussion pattern

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Bronchial breathing, increased fremitus, dull percussion, coarse crackles
Stony-dull percussion, absent breath sounds, reduced fremitus, trachea deviated away
Hyper-resonant, absent breath sounds, trachea deviated away (if tension)
Polyphonic expiratory wheeze, hyperexpansion, prolonged expiration

tips: Trachea deviates **towards** collapse/fibrosis but **away** from a big effusion or tension pneumothorax.
Stony-dull = effusion; just dull = consolidation.
Examine the back — most signs are best heard there.

obstetric-hx.summary: A pregnant woman with a problem, most often **bleeding after 24 weeks**: place the pregnancy (gestation, booking, scans, the placenta), characterise the bleed, and screen the two that kill, **placental abruption and placenta praevia**, and pre-eclampsia, before the obstetric and gynaecological background. Never a digital vaginal examination until a scan has excluded praevia (RCOG GTG 63).

sections.title: This pregnancy
items: Gestation (LMP, the dating scan, EDD); singleton or multiple; how it was conceived (assisted conception raises praevia and abruption risk)
Booking, bloods, **blood group and rhesus status**; the 20-week anomaly scan: **where is the placenta?** (a low-lying placenta is rescanned at 32 weeks, RCOG GTG 27a)
Problems so far: bleeding earlier on (threatened miscarriage raises later abruption risk), BP, glucose, admissions

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Placental abruption**: Is it painful? Is your tummy hard or tender? Any knock or fall? Do you smoke, or use any drugs?
**Placenta praevia**: Was it painless? Where did the 20-week scan say the placenta was? Any caesareans before?
**Major haemorrhage and shock**: How much blood: soaking pads, clots? Still bleeding? Dizzy or faint?
**Fetal compromise**: Is the baby moving as usual?
**Pre-eclampsia**: Any headache, problems with your vision, pain under the ribs, or sudden swelling of the face or hands?

sections.title: The bleed
items: When, how much (spotting; minor <50 mL that has settled; major 50–1000 mL; massive >1000 mL or shock: RCOG GTG 63), colour, clots, still bleeding?
**Painful or painless**; after sex or trauma; contractions; fluid as well (ruptured membranes)
**Fetal movements** now, compared with usual

sections.title: The obstetric and gynaecological background
items: Gravidity and parity, and each outcome: mode of delivery, **previous caesarean sections**, complications (abruption, praevia, PPH, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth), miscarriages and terminations
Cervical screening history; sexual health

sections.title: Then
items: PMH (hypertension, diabetes, clotting); drugs (aspirin, folic acid, anything teratogenic) · allergies
Social: smoking, alcohol, **drugs (cocaine)**, support, and **domestic abuse: ask when she is alone** (abdominal trauma causes abruption)
ICE: what she is most worried about (usually the baby)

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: **Painful** bleeding, a tense **"woody"** uterus, shock out of proportion to the visible loss (concealed bleeding), fetal distress
**Painless**, often recurrent, bright red bleeding; soft non-tender uterus, high or abnormal presenting part; low placenta on the 20-week scan
Bleeding as the membranes rupture, with sudden fetal compromise: the blood is the baby's
Cervical ectropion, polyp, infection, cervical cancer: often postcoital; speculum, and the smear history
Mucus with a little blood, with regular tightenings

redflags: Heavy bleeding or signs of shock (tachycardia, pallor, collapse)
Abdominal pain with a tense, tender uterus (abruption)
Headache, visual disturbance, upper abdominal pain or new swelling (pre-eclampsia)
tips: **No digital vaginal examination** until an ultrasound has excluded placenta praevia (RCOG GTG 63); a speculum is fine.

Abruption risk factors: **a previous abruption** (the strongest), pre-eclampsia, smoking, cocaine, trauma; praevia: **previous caesarean sections**, assisted conception, multiparity, age over 40 (RCOG GTG 63).
Every non-sensitised **RhD-negative** woman with an APH gets **anti-D**, with a Kleihauer test to size the dose (RCOG GTG 63).
Ask about fetal movements every time; and see her alone for part of it.

abdo-exam.summary: Inspect → palpate (light then deep) → the organs → percuss → auscultate. Southampton flags this as a common weak point — drill the organ palpation technique until fluent.

sections.title: General inspection
items: At rest: cachexia, jaundice, distension, discomfort
Around the bed: stoma bags, drains, catheter, nutritional supplements

sections.title: Hands & arms
items: Clubbing, leuconychia, koilonychia, palmar erythema, Dupuytren’s, **liver flap** (asterixis)
Bruising/excoriations; check for an AV fistula (dialysis)

sections.title: Face & neck
items: Eyes: jaundice (sclera), conjunctival pallor, xanthelasma, Kayser-Fleischer rings
Mouth: ulcers, angular stomatitis, glossitis, hydration
Palpate for **Virchow’s node** (left supraclavicular — gastric malignancy)

sections.title: Abdomen — inspect & palpate
items: Inspect: scars, distension, striae, caput medusae, visible masses/peristalsis; ask about pain first
Light palpation (all 9 regions) — tenderness, guarding, rebound
Deep palpation — masses; then the organs

sections.title: Organs
items: **Liver** — palpate from the RIF up towards the costal margin on inspiration
**Spleen** — from RIF towards left costal margin (roll to right side if not felt)
**Kidneys** — ballot bimanually
Palpate the **aorta** (expansile = AAA); percuss for **shifting dullness** (ascites)

sections.title: Auscultate
items: Bowel sounds (absent = ileus/peritonitis; tinkling = obstruction)
Bruits — aortic and renal

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Jaundice, ascites, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, liver flap
Massive splenomegaly (crosses midline, notch, can’t get above it)
Rigid abdomen, absent bowel sounds, rebound tenderness
Left supraclavicular (Virchow’s) node — Troisier’s sign — cachexia, epigastric mass

tips: Palpate the liver and spleen from the **RIF upwards** on inspiration — starting too high misses a big organ.
Distinguish spleen from kidney: spleen has a notch, moves with respiration, you can’t get above it, and is dull to percussion.
Always ask about pain and watch the face while palpating.

suturing.summary: Inject or topically apply a local anaesthetic. Understand the maximum doses of local anaesthetic agents.

sections.title: Why
items: Know the **maximum safe doses** (a classic examinable point) and how to recognise & manage **LA systemic toxicity (LAST)**.

sections.title: Indications
items: Infiltration anaesthesia for suturing, incision & drainage, cannulation of an awake site, minor procedures

sections.title: Equipment
items: Local anaesthetic (e.g. lidocaine 1% or 2%, ± adrenaline)
Syringe & needle; antiseptic

sections.title: Prepare
items: Check allergies; calculate the **maximum dose** for the patient’s weight
Clean the site

sections.title: Infiltrate
items: Insert the needle; **aspirate** to ensure not intravascular, then infiltrate slowly
Warn of a stinging sensation; wait for onset, then test before proceeding

sections.title: Why
items: Assess, clean, close appropriately, dress. Suturing must be demonstrable by **either a hand-held tie or an instrument tie** in the exam.

sections.title: Indications
items: Simple lacerations, surgical wound closure/dressing

sections.title: Equipment
items: Suture pack (needle holder, toothed forceps, scissors)
Suture material (appropriate gauge)
Local anaesthetic
Cleaning/irrigation solution, dressing

sections.title: Assess & prepare
items: Examine depth, contamination, neurovascular and tendon status; check tetanus
Clean and irrigate the wound thoroughly
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and test

sections.title: Close
items: Choose the method: **sutures**, adhesive strips (Steri-Strips), tissue glue, or staples
Load the needle ~⅔ from tip to thread in the needle holder
Pierce perpendicular (**90°**) ~4 mm from the wound edge, with **equal bites and depth** either side
Evert the edges, instrument-tie the knot (~3 throws), and space sutures evenly
Aim for good apposition without tension

sections.title: After
items: Apply a dressing; give wound-care and red-flag advice (infection)
Advise suture-removal timing: face ~5 days, scalp 7–10, limbs/trunk 10–14

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Lidocaine max: **3 mg/kg** (absolute max ~200 mg) plain; **7 mg/kg** (absolute max 500 mg) with adrenaline
LAST management: stop, ABCDE, 100% O₂, treat seizures, and **IV lipid emulsion 20%** (Intralipid)
Technique: needle **90°** to skin, ~4 mm bite from the edge, equal depth either side, edges everted
Suture removal: face ~5 days · scalp 7–10 · limbs/trunk 10–14 · over joints ~14
Suture choice: **non-absorbable monofilament** (nylon/polypropylene) for skin; absorbable (e.g. Vicryl) for deep/buried layers
Do not primarily close: mammalian bites, grossly contaminated, or wounds >6–12 h old

tips: Know max doses: **lidocaine 3 mg/kg plain (max ~200 mg), 7 mg/kg with adrenaline (max 500 mg)** (1% = 10 mg/mL).
Aspirate before injecting.
Recognise LAST and its management: stop, ABCDE, and **IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid)** — call for help.

diabetic-foot.summary: Look for ulcers and deformity, feel the pulses and temperature, test protective sensation with a 10 g monofilament and vibration, then give the NICE risk category. The foot check that prevents amputations.

sections.title: Look
items: Ulcers: between the toes, under the metatarsal heads, the heels
Calluses, deformity (claw toes, hallux valgus, **Charcot** foot), nails, fungal infection
Skin: colour, dryness, cracks, signs of infection
Footwear: fit, wear, foreign bodies

sections.title: Feel
items: Temperature (a hot, swollen foot without an ulcer = Charcot until proven otherwise)
Capillary refill
Pulses: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial

sections.title: Sensation
items: **10 g monofilament** at the standard sites on the sole, eyes closed — until it bends, 1–2 seconds
Vibration with a 128 Hz tuning fork at the big toe joint
Ankle reflexes

sections.title: Risk (NICE NG19)
items: Low: no risk factors
Moderate: neuropathy, deformity or non-critical ischaemia
High: previous ulcer or amputation, dialysis, or two of the above
**Active**: ulcer, spreading infection, critical ischaemia, gangrene or suspected Charcot — refer to the foot service within 1 working day

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Painless ulcer at a pressure point, warm foot, bounding pulses
Painful punched-out ulcer, cold foot, absent pulses
Hot, swollen, deformed foot, often painless
Charcot neuroarthropathy — urgent offload and refer

tips: Name the risk category out loud — it decides the follow-up.
Monofilament with the eyes closed, on the sole, not on callus.
A hot swollen foot in a diabetic is Charcot until proven otherwise.

explain-dx.summary: Pitch the explanation at the patient, using chunking and checking. Elicit and address their ideas, concerns and expectations, and make a shared plan.

sections.title: Prepare
items: Confirm identity; find out what they already know and want to know
Signpost — “I’d like to explain your diagnosis and what happens next.”

sections.title: Explain (chunk & check)
items: Give information in small chunks, plain language, avoiding jargon
**Check understanding** after each chunk — “Does that make sense so far?”
Use diagrams/analogies where helpful

sections.title: Explore ICE
items: Ideas — what do they think is going on?
Concerns — what are they most worried about?
Expectations — what were they hoping for today?

sections.title: Plan & safety-net
items: Agree a management plan together (shared decision-making)
Offer written information; safety-net; check questions; arrange follow-up

points: In words: the body doesn't respond to its insulin well, or make enough, so sugar builds up in the blood. Diagnosed at HbA1c 48 or above.
Why it matters: over years, the eyes, kidneys, nerves (feet) and heart and blood vessels.

What happens: lifestyle and weight loss (remission is possible), usually metformin; an HbA1c target of about 48 (53 on drugs that cause hypos); yearly eye screening, foot and kidney checks; structured education (DESMOND).
In words: the pressure in the arteries is too high; it has no symptoms, which is why it's checked.
Diagnosed: clinic 140/90 or more, confirmed with home or ambulatory readings of 135/85 or more.
Why it matters: raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease.

What happens: less salt (under 6 g a day), exercise, alcohol and weight; medicines (an ACE inhibitor or ARB under 55 or with diabetes; amlodipine at 55+ or of Black African or Caribbean family origin).
In words: the airways are sensitive and inflamed, so they narrow with triggers (colds, allergies, exercise, cold air, smoke).

What happens: a daily preventer (inhaled steroid) and a reliever, or one combined inhaler; inhaler technique; a written action plan; when to get help (a reliever not lasting 4 hours, can't finish a sentence: 999).
In words: lasting damage to the airways and lungs, usually from smoking; it doesn't go back, but it can be slowed.
What happens: stopping smoking is the single biggest thing; inhalers; pulmonary rehabilitation; flu, pneumococcal and COVID vaccines; a rescue pack and plan for flare-ups.
In words: the top chambers of the heart beat irregularly; it raises the risk of stroke about five-fold, because clots can form.
What happens: anticoagulation based on stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) weighed against bleeding; controlling the rate (beta-blocker) or the rhythm.
In words: the heart isn't pumping as strongly as it should, so fluid builds up (breathless, swollen ankles); not that the heart has stopped.
What happens: several medicines that improve how long and how well people live; weigh daily, and report a gain of 2 kg in 3 days or more breathlessness; a fluid plan; vaccines.
In words: a tendency to have seizures because of bursts of electrical activity in the brain.

What happens: medicines, avoiding triggers (sleep loss, alcohol); safety (showers not baths, no swimming alone); driving rules (see DVLA); SUDEP is rare but worth mentioning, and good control lowers it.

pitfalls: A jargon-heavy monologue with no checking.
Ignoring the patient’s concerns (ICE).
Not offering choice / shared decision-making.
No safety-netting or written information.

inhaler.summary: Explain to a patient how to use an inhaler correctly, including spacers, and check their technique is correct.

sections.title: Why
items: Poor inhaler technique is a leading cause of “uncontrolled” asthma. A teaching station — explain, demonstrate, then **check the patient does it**.

sections.title: Indications
items: Asthma & COPD — reliever and preventer inhalers

sections.title: Equipment
items: pMDI (metered-dose inhaler) ± spacer
Placebo device for demonstration

sections.title: pMDI technique
items: Remove the cap and **shake** the inhaler
Breathe out fully
Seal the lips around the mouthpiece
Press the canister while starting a **slow, deep** inhalation
Hold the breath for ~10 seconds
Wait ~30 seconds before a second dose

sections.title: With a spacer
items: Attach the inhaler to the spacer; one puff at a time
Either tidal breathing (5 breaths) or a single slow breath + 10-second hold
Spacers improve delivery and reduce oropharyngeal deposition

sections.title: Aftercare
items: Rinse the mouth after an inhaled **corticosteroid** (reduces oral candidiasis/hoarseness)
Check and correct the patient’s technique

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: pMDI: **slow, deep** inhalation while actuating; breath-hold ~10 s; wait ~30 s between doses
Always use a **spacer** for children and anyone with poor coordination; rinse the mouth after an inhaled steroid

tips: Get the patient to demonstrate back — technique-checking is marked.
Slow, deep breath (not fast) — a common error.
Rinse mouth after steroids; spacer for children/poor coordination.

back-hx.summary: Most back pain is mechanical, but the job of the history is to exclude the serious causes — cauda equina, malignancy, infection and fracture — via the red flags.

sections.title: Characterise (SOCRATES)
items: Site, onset (trauma?), character, radiation (down the leg = sciatica), timing (worse at night?), aggravating/relieving, severity

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Cauda equina**: Numb between the legs or around the bottom? Any change in your bladder, bowels or sexual function? Both legs?
**Spinal metastases**: Ever had cancer? Weight loss? Pain at night or at rest?
**Spinal infection**: Fever? Injecting drugs, immunosuppressed, a recent procedure?
**Fracture**: A fall or injury? Osteoporosis, long-term steroids?
**AAA**: Pain through to the back? Did you collapse or faint? A pulsing in the tummy? Over 65, a smoker, a known aneurysm?

sections.title: Red-flag screen (must ask)
items: **Cauda equina**: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness
Malignancy: age >50, weight loss, history of cancer, night pain
Infection: fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression
Fracture: trauma, osteoporosis, steroids

sections.title: Function & context
items: Impact on function/work, mood, prior episodes, occupation

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Cancer back pain** (came up 2024): a cancer history (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid, myeloma), **night pain, thoracic pain**, weight loss, and any weakness, numbness or bladder change. Spinal metastases without neurology: MRI within a week; **with neurological symptoms (MSCC): MRI within 24 hours** and dexamethasone (NICE NG234)

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Movement-related, no red flags, improves with activity
Radiating leg pain in a dermatome, positive straight-leg raise
Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, bilateral weakness — emergency
Age >50, weight loss, night pain, cancer history
Trauma/osteoporosis, or fever/IVDU with focal tenderness

redflags: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness (cauda equina — emergency MRI)
Weight loss / history of cancer / night pain (malignancy)
Significant trauma or age <20 / >55 with new pain
tips: Explicitly ask the **cauda equina** questions in every back-pain history — it’s a can’t-miss emergency.
Red flags drive imaging; without them, most back pain is managed conservatively.
Night pain + weight loss + cancer history should raise malignancy.

venepuncture.summary: Insert a needle into a vein to take a blood sample; ensure correct order of draw, correct containers, correct labelling, and prompt dispatch to the lab.

sections.title: Why
items: Bread-and-butter FY1 skill. Marks turn on **ANTT, order of draw, tourniquet timing and bedside labelling**.

sections.title: Indications
items: Blood tests for diagnosis & monitoring
Blood cultures (see separate)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Tourniquet
Vacutainer holder + needle (or butterfly)
Blood bottles (correct order)
Antiseptic wipe, gauze, tape, sharps bin

sections.title: Prepare
items: Confirm patient identity, consent, check allergies (e.g. plasters)
Wash hands, gloves; apply the tourniquet ~4 finger-widths above the site
Palpate a suitable vein (antecubital fossa — median cubital); clean and let dry

sections.title: Draw
items: Anchor the skin; insert bevel-up at ~15–30°
Fill bottles in the correct **order of draw**: blood cultures → coagulation (blue) → serum (gold) → heparin (green) → EDTA (purple) → fluoride (grey)
Release the tourniquet **before** removing the needle
Apply pressure; dispose of the sharp immediately

sections.title: After
items: Label bottles **at the bedside**; complete the request; send promptly

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Order of draw: blood cultures → coagulation (light blue) → serum (gold/red) → heparin (green) → EDTA (purple) → fluoride oxalate (grey)
Tourniquet on for **<1 minute** — prolonged stasis haemolyses the sample and falsely raises K⁺
Insert bevel-up at **15–30°**; release the tourniquet before withdrawing the needle

tips: Tourniquet **<1 minute** — prolonged application haemolyses the sample and falsely raises potassium.
Order of draw prevents cross-contamination of additives.
Label at the bedside — never pre-label or label away from the patient.

eol.summary: A clinical decision about ONE intervention, but one that must be **discussed** — failing to consult was unlawful in *Tracey*. The commonest error is letting the patient believe it means abandonment.

sections.title: Prepare
items: Know the clinical position: would CPR work, and what would survival look like? You cannot have the conversation without an answer.
Private space, sit down, offer to have family present if the patient wants them.

sections.title: Explore first
items: What do they understand about their illness and where it is heading?
What matters to them — being at home, staying independent, avoiding hospital, seeing someone in particular?

sections.title: Explain
items: Describe what CPR actually involves and, honestly, how likely it is to work for them.
State clearly that this is about ONE treatment, and that everything else continues.

sections.title: Decide and document
items: It is a clinical recommendation, not a request for consent — but it must be explained, and disagreement escalated to a senior.
Record the discussion, who was present, and the reasoning. Complete ReSPECT where used.

points: Chest compressions (ribs often break), shocks, and a breathing tube: an attempt to restart the heart after it has stopped.

Outcomes: in hospital, about 1 in 4 survive to go home (about half with a shockable rhythm, about 1 in 10 with asystole); far fewer with advanced illness or frailty, and some survivors have brain injury.
DNACPR is about CPR only: every other treatment continues ("this isn't about stopping care").
It's a clinical decision: a patient or family can't insist on CPR that won't work, but the patient must be told and involved unless that would cause them harm (Tracey, 2014).
Family: they're consulted, but don't decide, unless they hold an LPA for health and welfare; an advance decision refusing CPR is binding if valid.
Documented and reviewable; often part of a ReSPECT plan. Language that helps: "allow a natural death".
knowledge.source: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals (2014); BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN guidance on CPR decisions; ReSPECT

pitfalls: Asking “do you want us to resuscitate you?” — it is not a menu choice, and the question misleads.
Letting them think DNACPR means no antibiotics, no fluids, no escalation.
Making the decision without any discussion at all — unlawful, per *Tracey*.
Using “we would not be able to do anything for you” instead of naming what you WILL do.
Having the conversation for the first time when the patient is already peri-arrest.

msk-xr.summary: Present a fracture film the way you would on the phone to orthopaedics: **which bone, where, what pattern, how displaced**, and anything that changes management (open, intra-articular, pathological). For the hip, decide **intracapsular or extracapsular**, because that decides the operation (NICE CG124).

sections.title: Before you look
items: Patient, date, side marker; **two views** (AP and lateral), and the joints above and below for a long bone
Adequacy: the whole bone in view; exposure

sections.title: Describe the fracture
items: **Bone and location**: proximal, middle or distal third; the femoral neck, trochanters or shaft
**Pattern**: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted (more than two pieces), segmental; greenstick or buckle in a child
**Displacement**: translation, angulation, rotation, shortening, described by where the distal fragment has gone
Intra-articular? An open wound over it (an open fracture is an emergency: antibiotics, photograph, cover, theatre)?

sections.title: The hip on an AP pelvis and lateral
items: **Shenton's line** broken; the trabecular pattern of the neck interrupted; cortical breaks; a prominent lesser trochanter (the leg externally rotated)
**Intracapsular** (subcapital, transcervical: the blood supply to the head is at risk) or **extracapsular** (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric)
Compare with the other side; check the pubic rami, which can explain the same pain

sections.title: Pathological fracture
items: A fracture through abnormal bone after little force: a **lytic or sclerotic lesion**, thin cortex, a periosteal reaction
Metastases from breast, lung, kidney, thyroid and prostate; myeloma; osteoporosis

sections.title: Then say what you would do
items: Analgesia (a fascia iliaca block for a hip), neurovascular check distal to it, ortho referral
**Hip**: surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission (NICE CG124)
If you still suspect a hip fracture and the X-ray is normal: **MRI**, or CT if MRI is not available within 24 hours (NICE CG124)

pairs.title: Which hip operation (NICE CG124)
rows: Arthroplasty: total hip replacement if they walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick and are fit for it; otherwise hemiarthroplasty
Trochanteric (extracapsular), above and including the lesser trochanter
Sliding hip screw, in preference to a nail (except reverse oblique)
Mobilise the day after surgery, unless contraindicated (NICE CG124)

redflags: A cold, pale or pulseless limb, or numbness distal to the fracture
A femoral shaft fracture: blood loss can be over a litre
A spiral fracture in a child who is not yet walking (non-accidental injury)
A lesion at the fracture (pathological: look for the primary)
tips: Start: "This is an AP and lateral X-ray of the left femur of …, taken on …"; then the most important finding first.
Two views, two joints: one view can hide a displaced fracture.
Undisplaced intracapsular fractures are usually fixed with screws; the head's blood supply is the reason displaced ones are replaced instead.

gynae-hx.summary: Characterise the bleeding and place it in the reproductive context. The first split is pregnant vs not — always establish pregnancy status (β-hCG) and exclude an ectopic.

sections.title: Characterise
items: Amount (clots, flooding, pads/hour), timing (intermenstrual, postcoital, postmenopausal), duration, pain, associated discharge

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Ectopic pregnancy**: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period? Bleeding, pain on one side, shoulder-tip pain, feeling faint? A previous ectopic, PID or a coil?
**Heavy loss and shock**: How many pads, soaking through, clots? Dizzy or faint?
**Cancer**: Any bleeding after the menopause, after sex, or between periods? When was your last smear?
**Miscarriage with infection**: Fever, smelly discharge, pain?

sections.title: Reproductive context
items: LMP, cycle regularity, **pregnancy possibility / contraception**, smear history, parity
Postmenopausal bleeding = endometrial cancer until proven otherwise

sections.title: Screen
items: If pregnant: ectopic (unilateral pain, shoulder-tip), miscarriage, molar
If not: fibroids, polyps, PCOS, bleeding disorder, cervical/endometrial pathology

sections.title: The gynaecological frame
items: Menstrual: menarche, LMP, cycle length and duration, heaviness, pain; intermenstrual, postcoital, postmenopausal bleeding
Obstetric: gravidity and parity, outcomes
Contraception and HRT; sexual history; cervical screening history
Pain: dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, pelvic pain; discharge; prolapse; urinary and bowel symptoms

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Menopause symptoms** (came up 2024, as "difficulty sleeping, forgetful"): hot flushes and sweats, sleep, mood, memory and concentration, vaginal dryness and sex, urinary symptoms; last period. Diagnosed **without tests at 45 or over** (perimenopause: new vasomotor symptoms with a changed cycle; menopause: 12 months without a period); FSH only at 40 to 45, or under 40 (NICE NG23). Then the HRT conversation: VTE, breast cancer, stroke

**Bloating** (came up 2024): persistent or frequent (more than 12 times a month) bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary urgency = **ovarian cancer** until tested. At 40 or over: CA125 with **age-based thresholds** (35 at 40 to 49, 31 at 50 to 59, 24 at 60 to 69, 25 at 70 to 79, 31 at 80+) then urgent ultrasound; under 40: straight to urgent ultrasound. Ascites or a mass: suspected cancer referral (NICE NG12, 2026)

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Positive β-hCG, unilateral pain, amenorrhoea then bleeding — emergency
**Postmenopausal** bleeding — aged 55+: suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)

redflags: Postcoital bleeding with an abnormal cervix
tips: Establish **pregnancy status** first — it changes everything.
Postmenopausal bleeding at 55+ is a suspected cancer referral until endometrial cancer is excluded (NICE NG12).
Any pregnant woman with pain + bleeding = exclude ectopic urgently.

neuro-hx.summary: Distinguish primary headaches (migraine, tension, cluster) from the sinister secondary causes (SAH, meningitis, raised ICP, GCA). Onset and red flags are everything.

sections.title: Characterise
items: Onset (**thunderclap** = SAH), duration, frequency, character (throbbing/band/stabbing), site (unilateral/global), timing (worse in the morning = raised ICP)

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Subarachnoid haemorrhage**: Was it sudden, the worst ever, at full strength within a minute?
**Meningitis**: Fever, stiff neck, light hurting your eyes, a rash that doesn't fade, drowsy or confused?
**Raised pressure (tumour, bleed)**: Worse lying down, coughing or straining? Vomiting in the morning? Weakness, vision change, a fit?
**Giant cell arteritis**: Over 50 with a new headache: tender scalp, jaw pain when chewing, any change in vision?
**Carbon monoxide**: Does anyone at home have it too? Is it better away from home?
**Acute glaucoma**: A red, painful eye, haloes round lights?

sections.title: Associated
items: Aura, photophobia, nausea (migraine); neck stiffness, fever, rash (meningitis); visual change, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness (GCA); focal neurology; autonomic (cluster)

sections.title: Triggers & context
items: Triggers (foods, stress, screens), analgesic overuse, recent head injury, immunosuppression, age (>50 new headache = GCA/tumour)

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **TIA** (came up 2024, with a carotid result): sudden focal symptoms that resolved (face, arm, speech, vision, balance), how long, any still there, vascular risk factors and AF. **Aspirin 300 mg at once** and specialist review **within 24 hours**; no ABCD2 scoring (NICE NG128); carotid imaging, and endarterectomy for a symptomatic 50 to 99% stenosis

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Sudden thunderclap “worst ever”, peaks in seconds, neck stiffness
Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, non-blanching rash
>50y, temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss, raised ESR
Recurrent, throbbing, aura, photophobia, nausea, hours–days
Worse in the morning/on coughing, vomiting, focal signs, papilloedema

redflags: Morning headache with vomiting/focal signs (raised ICP)
tips: “Worst headache ever, sudden” = SAH until a normal CT (± LP for xanthochromia) excludes it.
New headache over 50 with visual symptoms = start steroids for GCA before the biopsy.
Ask about analgesic use — medication-overuse headache is common.

cn-exam.summary: Systematically test the 12 cranial nerves in order. The pattern of deficits localises the lesion — a single nerve, a brainstem level, or a supranuclear cause.

sections.title: I — Olfactory
items: Ask about any change in smell/taste (formal testing rarely required)

sections.title: II — Optic
items: Visual **acuity** (Snellen), **colour** (Ishihara), **fields** to confrontation, **inspection** (pupils)
Pupillary reflexes — direct, consensual, accommodation; **swinging-light** test for an RAPD
Fundoscopy (papilloedema, optic atrophy)

sections.title: III, IV, VI — Eye movements
items: Test the **H pattern** of gaze; ask about diplopia at extremes
III palsy: “down and out” eye, ptosis, fixed dilated pupil; IV: vertical diplopia on looking down; VI: failure of abduction

sections.title: V — Trigeminal
items: **Sensation** in all 3 divisions (ophthalmic/maxillary/mandibular)
**Motor**: clench teeth (masseter/temporalis), jaw jerk
Corneal reflex (offer)

sections.title: VII — Facial
items: Test all facial muscles: raise eyebrows, screw eyes shut, puff cheeks, show teeth
**Forehead spared = UMN** (stroke); forehead involved = LMN (Bell’s palsy)

sections.title: VIII — Vestibulocochlear
items: Gross hearing + whisper test; Rinne & Weber (512 Hz)

sections.title: IX, X — Glossopharyngeal & vagus
items: Say “ahh” — uvula deviates **away** from the side of a X lesion; gag reflex (offer); swallow/cough

sections.title: XI — Accessory
items: Shrug shoulders (trapezius) and turn head against resistance (sternocleidomastoid)

sections.title: XII — Hypoglossal
items: Inspect the tongue for wasting/fasciculation; protrude — deviates **towards** the side of the lesion

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Ptosis + “down and out” eye + fixed dilated pupil
Third nerve palsy (surgical — e.g. PComm aneurysm)
Tongue deviates towards the lesion; uvula deviates away

tips: The **forehead** is the key to VII: spared = UMN, involved = LMN.
Tongue **towards**, uvula **away** — memorise the directions.
Do the swinging-light test for an RAPD every time you test the pupils.

knee-exam.summary: Look → feel → move → special tests for the ligaments and menisci. A focused MSK exam following the look/feel/move framework.

sections.title: Look
items: Standing: valgus/varus, swelling, muscle (quadriceps) wasting; gait (antalgic)
Supine: scars, effusion, erythema

sections.title: Feel
items: Temperature; effusion (patellar tap / sweep test); joint-line tenderness (meniscus); popliteal fossa (Baker’s cyst)

sections.title: Move
items: Active then passive flexion/extension; note range, crepitus, fixed flexion

sections.title: Special tests
items: **Anterior/posterior draw & Lachman** (cruciate ligaments)
**Valgus/varus stress** (collateral ligaments)
McMurray’s (meniscus)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Positive anterior draw / Lachman, often after a “pop” and rapid effusion
Effusion, crepitus, reduced range, varus deformity in an older patient

tips: Always examine the joint above and below.
Lachman’s is the most sensitive ACL test.
A rapid tense effusion after trauma suggests haemarthrosis (ACL/fracture).

axr.summary: Small bowel or large bowel, how dilated, and the emergencies: obstruction, volvulus, perforation, toxic megacolon.

sections.title: Read
items: Details; usually an AP supine film
Bowel gas: small bowel is central with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width; large bowel is peripheral with haustra
**3–6–9 rule**: small bowel >3 cm, colon >6 cm, caecum >9 cm = dilated
Outside the bowel: calcification, stones, bones, free gas

pairs.title: Patterns
rows: Coffee-bean loop from the left iliac fossa
Both sides of the bowel wall visible (Rigler's sign)

tips: Perforation is better seen on an erect chest X-ray.

urinalysis.summary: Explain how to collect a midstream urine sample; test urine to detect abnormalities; perform a pregnancy test where appropriate.

sections.title: Why
items: A rapid screen — but interpret in context (asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in the elderly and shouldn’t be treated on dipstick alone).

sections.title: Indications
items: Suspected UTI
Haematuria, proteinuria
Assessing an unwell/septic patient
Screening in pregnancy

sections.title: Equipment
items: Reagent dipstick (in date)
Sterile MSU pot
Gloves; timer

sections.title: Collect
items: Explain a **midstream** clean-catch: clean, void the first part, then catch the mid-stream
Use a fresh sample (test within a few hours; refrigerate otherwise)

sections.title: Test
items: Dip the strip fully, remove immediately, tap off excess
Read each pad at the **correct time** against the colour chart
Perform a β-hCG pregnancy test where relevant

sections.title: Interpret
items: Nitrites (Gram-negatives) + leucocytes → supports UTI
Blood, protein → renal/urological workup
Glucose/ketones → diabetes; send MSU for culture if infection suspected

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Nitrites + leucocytes → likely UTI. **Do not** diagnose UTI on dipstick alone in the over-65s or catheterised — send an MSU
Dipstick has limited value over 65; asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and should not be treated

tips: Read pads at the **timed** intervals — reading too early/late changes the result.
Don’t diagnose UTI on dipstick alone in the elderly/catheterised.
Offer a pregnancy test where the scenario allows.

mse.summary: Observe and present the mental state in a fixed order, then a **risk assessment** — always. The MSE is what you see now; the psychiatric history is the background.

sections.title: The MSE, in order
items: **Appearance and behaviour** — self-care, dress, psychomotor activity, eye contact, rapport
**Speech** — rate, rhythm, volume, quantity (pressured, poverty of speech)
**Mood** (in their words) and **affect** (what you observe: reactive, blunted, flat, incongruent)
**Thought form** (flight of ideas, loosening of associations, thought block, perseveration) and **content** (delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal thoughts)
**Perception** — hallucinations (which modality; second or third person), illusions
**Cognition** — orientation, attention, short-term memory
**Insight and judgement**

sections.title: Risk (never skip)
items: To self: thoughts of self-harm or suicide — **ideation → plan → intent → means**, previous attempts; self-neglect
To others, and from others (exploitation, safeguarding)
Protective factors. Asking directly does not increase risk

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Rapid jumps with understandable links — mania
Fixed, false belief, out of keeping with culture, held despite evidence
Perception without a stimulus vs misperception of a real one

tips: Present in the same order every time — it reads as competence.
Quote the patient for mood (“I feel empty”).
Always the risk assessment, and a plan for it (crisis team, senior).
The CSE Paper A asks for exactly this write-up — practise both.

alcohol-hx.summary: Quantify (units, pack-years), screen with a named tool, look for dependence and withdrawal, and offer help without lecturing.

sections.title: Alcohol
items: Type, amount, pattern; units: **ABV% × volume (L)**
**AUDIT-C** first (5+ = increasing risk → full AUDIT; AUDIT 20+ suggests possible dependence)
Dependence: tolerance, withdrawal, morning drinking, drinking taking priority
Withdrawal: seizures, delirium tremens; harm: liver, falls, work, family

sections.title: Smoking
items: **Pack-years** = cigarettes a day ÷ 20 × years smoked
Vaping; previous quit attempts

sections.title: Units
items: Weekly guideline — No more than 14 units, spread over 3 or more days (UK CMO)
Pint of 5% lager — ≈ 2.8 units
750 mL bottle of 13% wine — ≈ 9.75 units
70 cL bottle of 40% spirit — 28 units

tips: Never advise abrupt cessation in dependence — withdrawal can kill.
Show the unit working.

immunisation.summary: Explain what the vaccines are, when they're given, their side effects and the myths, and answer the parent's real worry.

sections.title: The schedule (England)
items: Primary course at **8, 12 and 16 weeks** (6-in-1 and others); boosters around 1 year, including MMR; preschool boosters; teenage HPV, 3-in-1 and MenACWY
The schedule changed in 2025–26 (including MMRV): **check the current NHS schedule** before quoting exact ages

sections.title: Side effects
items: Common: sore arm, fever, irritability
**Paracetamol after MenB** in babies (three doses) to reduce fever (NHS)
Rare: anaphylaxis (staff trained, observed)

sections.title: Concerns
items: MMR does not cause autism — the study was fraudulent and retracted
Contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose; live vaccines in significant immunosuppression

sections.title: Tips
items: Ask what they've heard and where.
Respect the decision; keep the door open.

sensitive.summary: Stay calm, acknowledge the anger explicitly, and find the underlying concern. Don’t get defensive — listen, empathise, and offer a constructive way forward.

sections.title: Set up safely
items: Ensure a safe environment (exit accessible, consider a colleague); sit at the same level
Introduce yourself calmly and give them your full attention

sections.title: Acknowledge & explore
items: **Name the emotion** — “I can see you’re really angry, and I want to understand why.”
Let them vent without interrupting; listen actively
Explore the underlying concern — often fear, poor communication, or a genuine error

sections.title: Empathise & respond
items: Validate their feelings; **apologise** for any distress/failing (an apology is not an admission of liability)
Be honest; don’t make promises you can’t keep or become defensive

sections.title: Resolve & safety-net
items: Agree a concrete next step; explain what you’ll do
Offer PALS/complaints routes; document; escalate if a genuine safety/candour issue

pitfalls: Getting defensive or matching their tone.
Dismissing or minimising the concern.
Failing to acknowledge the emotion before problem-solving.
Not offering a concrete next step or escalation route.

cannulation.summary: Insert a cannula into a patient's vein and apply an appropriate dressing.

sections.title: Why
items: IV access for fluids, drugs and blood. Choose the **right gauge** for the job, confirm patency by flushing, and secure well.

sections.title: Indications
items: IV fluids, medications, blood products, contrast

sections.title: Equipment
items: Cannula (appropriate gauge)
Tourniquet, antiseptic, ANTT dressing, saline flush
Sharps bin, tape/securement

sections.title: Prepare
items: Confirm identity, consent, allergies; wash hands, gloves
Apply the tourniquet; select a suitable vein (back of hand/forearm; avoid joints and the dominant hand where possible)
Clean the skin and let it dry

sections.title: Cannulate
items: Anchor the skin; insert bevel-up at ~15–30° until flashback
Advance slightly, then slide the cannula off the needle into the vein
Release the tourniquet; withdraw the needle into the sharps bin
Cap, then **flush with saline** to confirm patency (no pain/swelling)
Secure with a sterile dressing; label with the date

sections.title: Aftercare
items: Document; monitor the site (VIP score) for phlebitis/extravasation

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Approx. flow rates: grey 16G ~200 mL/min · green 18G ~90 · pink 20G ~60 · blue 22G ~36 (bigger gauge number = smaller bore)
Grey/green for rapid fluids, blood and resuscitation; pink/blue for routine access

tips: Match the gauge to the need: **grey 16G/green 18G** (rapid fluids/blood), **pink 20G/blue 22G** (routine).
Flush to confirm patency — a key safety step.
Release the tourniquet before removing the needle; date the dressing.

pvd-exam.summary: Inspect → palpate pulses & temperature → auscultate for bruits → special tests (Buerger’s). Localises the level of arterial disease in the limb.

sections.title: Inspect
items: Colour (pallor), trophic changes (hair loss, shiny skin), **ulcers** (arterial: punched-out, painful, pressure points), gangrene, scars, missing toes
Between the toes and the heels (pressure areas)

sections.title: Palpate
items: Temperature (cool distally); capillary refill
Pulses: femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis (and radial/brachial in the arm)
Abdominal aorta (expansile = AAA)

sections.title: Auscultate & special
items: Bruits over the femoral and abdominal aorta
**Buerger’s test**: lift the leg to the angle of pallor, then hang down (reactive hyperaemia = sunset foot)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Absent foot pulses, punched-out painful ulcer at a pressure point, cool foot
Peripheral arterial disease / critical limb ischaemia
Sudden painful, pale, pulseless, cold, paraesthetic, paralysed limb
Buerger’s angle <20° with sunset rubor on dependency

tips: Arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, at pressure points; venous are shallow at the gaiter area.
Acute limb ischaemia (6 Ps) is a surgical emergency — don’t miss it.
Always feel for an AAA when examining the legs.

ecg-interp.summary: Read every ECG in the same order, describe before you interpret, and **act** on the finding. Spot the emergency first: STEMI, complete heart block, hyperkalaemia, VT.

sections.title: Before the waves
items: Patient details, date and time, symptoms at the time; calibration **25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV**

sections.title: In order
items: **Rate**: 300 ÷ large squares between R waves (regular), or QRS complexes in the 10-second strip × 6
**Rhythm**: regular? a P wave before every QRS?
**Axis**: leads I and aVF both positive = normal; I positive, aVF negative (and II negative) = left; I negative, aVF positive = right
**P waves**; **PR interval** 120–200 ms; **QRS** <120 ms
**ST segments**, **T waves**, **QTc**

sections.title: Then act
items: Name the finding, the likely cause and the immediate action (e.g. STEMI → primary PCI; hyperkalaemia → calcium gluconate, insulin–glucose)

pairs.title: Patterns
rows: ST elevation in II, III, aVF
PR lengthening then a dropped beat
Mobitz II — risk of complete block
Tall tented T, flat P, broad QRS
Broad QRS, W in V1 and M in V6
LBBB (“WiLLiaM”); M in V1, W in V6 = RBBB (“MaRRoW”)
Widespread saddle ST elevation, PR depression
The commonest ECG finding in PE

tips: Say the order out loud before you look for the answer.
A new LBBB with chest pain is treated like a STEMI.
Always end with what you'd do.

ecg-record.summary: Set up a recording of the electrical activity of the heart, ensuring all leads are correctly placed.

sections.title: Why
items: Correct **lead placement** is a patient-safety issue — misplacement mimics or masks ischaemia. Know the chest-lead landmarks cold.

sections.title: Indications
items: Chest pain, palpitations, syncope, breathlessness
Suspected ACS/arrhythmia; pre-op; electrolyte/drug effects

sections.title: Equipment
items: ECG machine + fresh electrodes
Razor & wipes (skin prep)

sections.title: Prepare
items: Confirm identity; expose the chest, wrists, ankles; position semi-recumbent
Clean/shave skin for good contact

sections.title: Place leads
items: Limb leads: Red→Right arm, yeLLow→Left arm, Green→left leg (foot), blacK→right leg (“Ride Your Green Bike”)
V1: 4th intercostal space, right sternal edge
V2: 4th ICS, left sternal edge
V4: 5th ICS, mid-clavicular line
V3: midway between V2 and V4
V5: anterior axillary line, same horizontal as V4
V6: mid-axillary line, same horizontal as V4

sections.title: Record
items: Check calibration (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV); minimise artefact
Print; label with name, DOB, date/time and whether symptomatic
Interpret systematically: rate, rhythm, axis, P-QRS-T, intervals, ischaemia

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Standard calibration: paper speed **25 mm/s**, amplitude **10 mm/mV** (1 large square = 0.2 s)
V1 = 4th ICS right sternal edge · V2 = 4th ICS left sternal edge · V4 = 5th ICS mid-clavicular line · V6 = mid-axillary, level with V4

tips: Lead placement is the marked skill — recite the V1–V6 landmarks.
Always **label** the trace (name/DOB/time/symptoms).
State the calibration and read systematically.

transfusion.summary: Understand safe transfusion practice and be able to discuss it with a doctor. Assessed as TWO sign-offs — the e-learning and a professional conversation — not by administering blood.

sections.title: Why
items:
Assessed as **two separate sign-offs, one each**:

· **24a — Blood Transfusion e-Learning** for doctors and non-medical authorisers of blood components.
· **24b — Blood transfusion professional conversation**, discussed with a relevant doctor.

There is **no simulated administration** to be signed off, which is what this page previously implied. The knowledge below is what the conversation covers, and the dominant theme is **patient safety** — the bedside identity check is what prevents the catastrophic ABO-incompatible (“wrong blood in patient”) reaction.

sections.title: Indications
items: Symptomatic anaemia — restrictive threshold **70 g/L** (target 70–90 g/L after), or **80 g/L** in acute coronary syndrome
Major haemorrhage

sections.title: Equipment
items: Valid group & save / crossmatched component
Blood-administration giving set (integral filter)
Prescription, observation chart

sections.title: Prepare
items: Ensure a valid sample & prescription; gain consent; take **baseline observations**
Ensure IV access (green/pink cannula) is patent

sections.title: The bedside check (critical)
items: Positively identify the patient — ask them to state name & DOB
Two-person check: patient wristband ↔ compatibility label ↔ the unit (blood group, donation number, expiry)
Any discrepancy → do **not** transfuse

sections.title: Transfuse & monitor
items: Start slowly; observations at 15 minutes, then per policy, and at the end
Complete each unit within **4 hours** of leaving the fridge
Watch for a reaction — fever, rigors, hypotension, breathlessness, loin/chest pain

sections.title: Reactions
items: Stop the transfusion, maintain IV access, ABCDE, re-check identity/unit
Escalate; distinguish acute haemolytic (ABO) / TACO / TRALI / febrile / allergic-anaphylactic

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Transfusion threshold 70 g/L (target 70–90 g/L); 80 g/L in acute coronary syndrome
Start a unit within 30 min of leaving the fridge; complete within 4 hours
Observations: before, at 15 min, then per policy, and at completion

tips: The **bedside positive-ID check** is the exam’s core safety point — never skip it.
Unit up within 30 min of leaving the fridge; finished within 4 hours.
Know the reaction types and the immediate “stop + ABCDE + escalate” response.

cse-rx-read.summary: Write a safe, legal, unambiguous prescription — an inpatient drug chart from a guideline and BNF excerpts, or discharge medicines (a TTO) — as an FY1 would. 20 minutes, BNF allowed.

sections.title: Before writing
items: Patient details on every sheet: name, DOB, hospital number, address, ward
**Allergies** (and the reaction) first — then weight and renal/hepatic function
Read the guideline or the notes for what to continue, stop or change, and why

sections.title: Every prescription
items: **Generic** name, dose, route, frequency, start date; duration for antibiotics and short courses
No abbreviations for units or micrograms; legible; signed, dated, bleep
PRN: the indication, the dose, the minimum interval and the **maximum in 24 hours**
Don't forget: VTE prophylaxis, regular medicines, analgesia, laxatives with opioids, anti-emetics

sections.title: Controlled drugs (TTO)
items: Drug, **form**, **strength**, dose, and the **total quantity in words and figures** (“56 (fifty-six) 30 mg capsules”)
Patient name and address; prescriber signature and date; valid for 28 days

sections.title: Syringe driver (CSCI over 24 h)
items: Each drug, its dose over 24 hours, the diluent (usually water for injection) and the volume; the start time
Breakthrough doses prescribed separately as PRN (often about a sixth of the 24-hour opioid dose)

tips: Check allergies before anything else — a prescription for an allergen is a critical error.
Write “units” and “micrograms” in full.
Laxative with every regular opioid.

hand-exam.summary: Look → feel → move → function → special tests. The pattern of joint involvement separates rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and psoriatic/gout.

sections.title: Look
items: Dorsum: swelling, deformity (ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb), muscle wasting, skin/nails (psoriasis, nail pitting)
Palms: wasting of thenar/hypothenar eminence, palmar erythema
Elbows: rheumatoid nodules, psoriatic plaques

sections.title: Feel
items: Temperature; palpate each joint (MCP, PIP, DIP, wrist) for **synovitis/tenderness**
Squeeze across the MCPs (tender in active RA); check the anatomical snuffbox; median/ulnar sensation

sections.title: Move & function
items: Active then passive: wrist flex/extend, finger flex/extend, thumb opposition
Function: grip, pincer, pick up a small object, undo a button

sections.title: Special tests
items: Tinel’s / Phalen’s for carpal tunnel; test median (thumb abduction) and ulnar (finger abduction) motor function

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Symmetrical MCP/PIP swelling, ulnar deviation, sparing DIPs
Bouchard’s (PIP) and Heberden’s (DIP) nodes, squaring of the thumb
Thenar wasting + reduced thumb abduction + positive Tinel/Phalen

tips: DIP involvement points away from RA (towards OA/psoriatic).
Always assess **function**, not just the joints — it drives management.
Squeeze the MCPs — tenderness suggests active synovitis.

spirometry.summary: Obstructive or restrictive, how severe, and whether it reverses.

sections.title: Read
items: **Obstructive**: FEV₁/FVC <0.7 (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis)
**Restrictive**: FEV₁/FVC normal or high, FVC <80% predicted (ILD, neuromuscular, chest wall, obesity)
Reversibility (after bronchodilator) supports asthma
TLCO (gas transfer): low in emphysema and ILD

tips: State the ratio first.

vte.summary: Every adult admitted to hospital is assessed for **VTE risk and bleeding risk** on admission (or by the first consultant review), on a national tool, then **reassessed at consultant review or when they change**. Prophylaxis is offered when the VTE risk outweighs the bleeding risk (NICE NG89).

sections.title: When
items: As soon as possible after admission, or by the time of the first consultant review, using a tool published by a national UK body (the Department of Health tool is the usual one) (NICE NG89)
**Reassess** at consultant review or if the clinical condition changes (NICE NG89)

sections.title: VTE risk
items: Mobility: significantly reduced (3 days or more), or expected to be
Surgery (especially orthopaedic, and long operations), trauma, a lower limb in plaster
Active cancer or cancer treatment; a previous VTE; a known thrombophilia; first-degree relative with VTE
Age over 60, obesity (BMI over 30), dehydration, critical care, significant medical illness (heart failure, inflammatory conditions)
Oestrogen (the combined pill, HRT); pregnancy or up to 6 weeks postpartum

sections.title: Bleeding risk
items: Active bleeding, or an acquired or untreated inherited bleeding disorder
Already on full anticoagulation (prophylaxis is not added)
Low platelets; acute stroke; uncontrolled systolic hypertension; recent neurosurgery, spinal or eye surgery; an LP or epidural expected within hours

sections.title: What to offer
items: **Pharmacological**: LMWH first line (fondaparinux if LMWH is contraindicated); doses adjusted for weight and renal function
**Mechanical**: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression, when drugs are contraindicated or alongside them in surgery
Tell the patient why, its risks, how to use it, and how to reduce their own risk (keep hydrated and mobile) (NICE NG89)

pairs.title: Durations (NICE NG89)
rows: LMWH for a minimum of 7 days, when the VTE risk outweighs bleeding
LMWH 10 days then aspirin for 28 days; or LMWH 28 days with stockings until discharge; or rivaroxaban
Aspirin for 14 days; or LMWH 14 days with stockings until discharge; or rivaroxaban
Fragility fracture of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur
LMWH (6 to 12 hours after surgery) or fondaparinux, for a month
No stockings; consider intermittent pneumatic compression, started within 3 days, for 30 days or until mobile or discharged

redflags: Stockings in peripheral arterial disease, after arterial bypass, in peripheral neuropathy or with fragile skin: do not (NICE NG89)
Prophylaxis prescribed on top of treatment-dose anticoagulation
A falling platelet count on heparin (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)
tips: Say both sides out loud: "Her VTE risk is…, her bleeding risk is…, so I would…".
Check weight and renal function before prescribing LMWH.
People on anticoagulants for an acute coronary syndrome do not usually need extra VTE prophylaxis (NICE NG89).

thyroid-exam.summary: Assess the neck lump (inspect → palpate → percuss → auscultate → swallow/tongue) AND the thyroid status (signs of hyper- or hypothyroidism), then state your clinical impression.

sections.title: Neck lump
items: Inspect from the front; ask to **swallow** (thyroid moves up) and **protrude the tongue** (thyroglossal cyst moves up)
Palpate from **behind**: size, consistency, nodularity, tenderness; assess tracheal deviation and lymph nodes
Percuss for retrosternal extension; **auscultate** for a bruit (Graves’)

sections.title: Thyroid status — hands & face
items: Hands: fine tremor, sweating, warm/cool, palmar erythema, thyroid acropachy, pulse (AF/tachy vs brady)
Eyes: **exophthalmos, lid lag, lid retraction, ophthalmoplegia** (Graves’)
Face: hair, skin (dry/coarse), expression

sections.title: Reflexes & legs
items: Reflexes: brisk (hyper) vs slow-relaxing (hypo)
Pretibial myxoedema (Graves’), proximal myopathy

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Diffuse goitre + bruit + exophthalmos + pretibial myxoedema
Single firm nodule that moves on swallowing
Midline lump that moves up on tongue protrusion
Bradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes, dry skin, coarse features
Tremor, warm sweaty palms, AF, lid lag

tips: Palpate the thyroid from **behind**; always ask the patient to swallow.
Swallowing moves a thyroid lump; tongue protrusion moves a thyroglossal cyst.
Comment on thyroid *status* (clinically eu-/hyper-/hypothyroid), not just the lump.

fundoscopy.summary: Perform basic ophthalmoscopy and identify common abnormalities.

sections.title: Why
items: Fundoscopy — a discriminating FY1 skill and directly relevant to the ophthalmology-adjacent presentations (red eye, sudden vision loss). Master the systematic sweep: **red reflex → optic disc → vessels → macula**.

sections.title: Indications
items: Assessing the red reflex (cataract, retinoblastoma in children)
Diabetic & hypertensive retinopathy
Papilloedema (raised ICP)
Sudden visual loss (central retinal artery/vein occlusion)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Direct ophthalmoscope (check the light and battery)
Mydriatic drops (e.g. tropicamide 1%) if dilation permitted
A darkened room

sections.title: Prepare
items: Dim the lights; dilate the pupil if appropriate and consented
Set the ophthalmoscope to 0 dioptres; ask the patient to fix on a distant point

sections.title: Examine
items: Use your **right** eye/hand for the patient’s **right** eye (and left for left)
Elicit the red reflex from ~arm’s length
Approach ~15° temporally, following a blood vessel back to the optic disc
Assess the disc — colour, margins, cup:disc ratio
Follow the four vascular arcades; assess AV nipping/haemorrhages/exudates
Finally ask the patient to look at the light to view the macula

tips: Right-to-right, left-to-left — getting the wrong eye/hand loses easy marks.
An **absent red reflex** is a red flag (cataract; leukocoria = retinoblastoma in a child).
Comment on the disc systematically; “I would ideally dilate for a full view” shows good practice.

early-preg.summary: Telling someone about a miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy: bad news skills, clear options, and the emotional support. It is not their fault — say so.

sections.title: The news
items: SPIKES; warning shot; plain words (“the pregnancy is not continuing”); silence

sections.title: Miscarriage options
items: Expectant (wait 7–14 days), medical (misoprostol ± mifepristone), surgical
Anti-D: not before 12 weeks; at 12+0 to 12+6 weeks if RhD-negative and having medical or surgical management (NICE NG126, 2026)

sections.title: Ectopic options
items: Methotrexate if suitable (unruptured, little pain, no heartbeat, hCG low — NICE NG126)
Surgery (salpingectomy) otherwise or if unstable

sections.title: Safety-net and support
items: Heavy bleeding, worsening pain, fever, feeling faint: come straight back
The Miscarriage Association; follow-up; future pregnancies

sections.title: Tips
items: Explicitly: nothing she did caused this.
Ask if she wants her partner present.

points: Expectant: wait 7–14 days for it to pass naturally; a pregnancy test at 3 weeks.
Medical: for a missed miscarriage, mifepristone, then misoprostol 48 hours later; for an incomplete one, misoprostol alone. Bleeding usually starts within 2–3 days.
Surgical: manual vacuum aspiration under local anaesthetic, or under general anaesthetic.
