Anti-D: not before 12 weeks; at 12+0 to 12+6 weeks if RhD-negative and having medical or surgical management.
Expectant: if stable and pain-free, a mass under 35 mm with no heartbeat, and hCG 1,000 or less (an option up to 1,500); hCG on days 2, 4 and 7.

Methotrexate: offered if hCG is under 1,500, no significant pain, a mass under 35 mm, no heartbeat; a choice with surgery from 1,500 to 5,000; hCG on days 4 and 7, then weekly. Avoid pregnancy for 3 months after (RCOG).

Surgery: first line with significant pain, a mass of 35 mm or more, a heartbeat, or hCG 5,000 or more; laparoscopic salpingectomy (salpingotomy if the other tube is damaged); an emergency if ruptured.
Come back for heavy bleeding (soaking a pad an hour), severe pain, fever or smelly discharge, feeling faint.
The early pregnancy unit; the Miscarriage Association; the chances of a healthy pregnancy next time are good.

colleague.summary: Patient first, then candour, then the system. You are not required to be certain — only to act. The trap is loyalty, or a conversation that becomes about blame.

sections.title: Patient first
items: Address the clinical consequence before anything else. Tell a senior immediately.

sections.title: Speak to the colleague
items: Privately, non-accusatory, curious rather than certain — you may be missing context.
Describe what you observed, not what you concluded about them.

sections.title: Candour to the patient
items: The patient must be told what happened, apologised to, and told what will be done — by the appropriate person, promptly.

sections.title: The system
items: Incident report. If it is a pattern, or the colleague may be unwell or impaired, escalate to the educational or clinical supervisor.
If patient safety remains at risk and local escalation fails: freedom to speak up guardian, medical director, ultimately the GMC.

pitfalls: Saying nothing out of loyalty or fear.
Confronting publicly, or in front of the patient.
Concluding intent — “you were careless” — rather than describing the observation.
Reporting and not telling the patient, or telling the patient and not reporting.
Believing you must be certain before acting. You must not be.

eye-exam.summary: Acuity, colour, fields, movements, pupils, then fundoscopy. The visual field defect tells you where the lesion is.

sections.title: Acuity and colour
items: **Snellen** at 6 m, each eye, with glasses; record as e.g. 6/9; pinhole if reduced
**Ishihara** plates for colour (optic nerve)

sections.title: Fields
items: Sit 1 m away at eye level; patient covers the opposite eye to you
Bring a target (finger or red pin) in from each quadrant; check for a central scotoma and the blind spot

sections.title: Movements
items: The **H pattern**; ask about double vision; watch for nystagmus

sections.title: Pupils
items: Size and shape; direct and consensual reflexes; **swinging light** for an RAPD; accommodation

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Optic tract, radiation or occipital cortex (stroke)

tips: Acuity first, always: it's the vital sign of the eye.
Do the swinging light test every time.

cse-ward-round.summary: Write the entry you would make in the notes during a post-take ward round: the key history, results, the consultant's diagnosis, a numbered plan, and the practical details that make it a legal record and keep the patient moving.

sections.title: The header
items: Patient name, DOB, NHS/hospital number
Date, time, **who is leading** (consultant), that it is the post-take ward round

sections.title: The body
items: **HPC**: the presenting symptom with the descriptors that matter (site, radiation, character, timing, what eased it), pain-free now?
Relevant background only: risk factors, PMH, drugs
**Results**: ECG, bloods (with trends, e.g. troponin 35 → 250), imaging — it shows the consultant reviewed them
**Impression / diagnosis**
**Plan**, numbered: investigations, treatment (drug, dose), referrals, monitoring, ceiling of care

sections.title: The footer
items: What the patient was told
**Triage specialty** and **estimated date of discharge**
Your name, grade, bleep, signature

tips: A reader should reach the same diagnosis from your notes — without a full re-history.
Write the plan as a numbered list of actions.
Current ACS treatment is aspirin with ticagrelor (or prasugrel/clopidogrel) plus fondaparinux, a factor Xa inhibitor (not an LMWH, as the 2019 model answer calls it).

hip-exam.summary: Look → feel → move → special tests (Trendelenburg, Thomas). Gait and leg-length assessment localise the problem.

sections.title: Look
items: Gait (antalgic, Trendelenburg); standing posture, pelvic tilt, muscle wasting
Supine: scars, deformity, leg length (true vs apparent)

sections.title: Feel
items: Temperature; palpate the greater trochanter (bursitis) and the joint

sections.title: Move
items: Flexion, extension, abduction/adduction, internal/external rotation (active then passive); note range and pain

sections.title: Special tests
items: **Trendelenburg** (abductor weakness — pelvis drops on the *opposite* side)
**Thomas test** (fixed flexion deformity)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Antalgic gait, reduced internal rotation, groin pain, crepitus
Weak hip abductors (superior gluteal nerve / arthritis)
Shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall
Lateral hip pain, tender greater trochanter

tips: In Trendelenburg the pelvis drops on the side **opposite** the weak abductors.
A shortened, externally rotated leg = fractured NOF until proven otherwise.
Reduced internal rotation is often the earliest sign of hip OA.

consent.summary: Valid consent = capacity + information + voluntariness. Explain the procedure, its benefits, risks and alternatives (incl. doing nothing), and check understanding — per Montgomery, tailored to what matters to this patient.

sections.title: Confirm the basics
items: Confirm identity and that you’re the right person to consent (or would escalate)
Assess **capacity** for this decision (understand, retain, weigh, communicate)

sections.title: Explain the procedure
items: What it involves, why it’s recommended, and the intended benefit
The **material risks** (common and serious) — per **Montgomery**, what a reasonable patient in their position would want to know
Alternatives, including the option of doing nothing

sections.title: Check & decide
items: Check understanding; answer questions; ensure the decision is voluntary (no coercion)
Confirm consent and document; provide written information

points: Valid consent: informed, voluntary, and from someone with capacity; it can be withdrawn at any point.
Montgomery (2015): tell them the material risks: what a reasonable person in their position would want to know, and what this patient would. Include the alternatives, and doing nothing.
No capacity: decide in their best interests under the Mental Capacity Act (consent form 4); an LPA for health or an advance decision may apply.
knowledge.source: Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015); GMC decision making and consent (2020); Mental Capacity Act 2005

points: Sore throat after; bloating. Perforation about 1 in 10,000 (more with dilatation); bleeding with biopsy rare.
Sedation: no driving, alcohol or important decisions for 24 hours; someone to take them home.
knowledge.source: BSG; typical NHS trust endoscopy leaflets (figures vary by trust)

points: Bowel prep the day before (a low-residue diet first). Perforation about 1 in 1,000 (more with polyp removal); bleeding after polyp removal about 1 in 100 (needing a transfusion, far fewer); occasionally incomplete or a lesion missed.
Sedation: as for an OGD.
knowledge.source: UK colonoscopy quality standards (Rees et al., Gut 2016); NHS trust leaflets

points: Common, usually mild: fever, itch or rash.
Serious and rare: the wrong blood (why the checks happen), fluid overload (TACO), a severe allergic reaction; infection is very rare (under 1 in a million for HIV and hepatitis).
Alternatives: iron, cell salvage. Respect a refusal (Jehovah's Witnesses) if they have capacity.
knowledge.source: SHOT annual report; NHS Blood and Transplant patient information

points: A headache after in up to about 1 in 3 (lying flat doesn't prevent it); back pain; bleeding, infection and nerve damage are rare.
knowledge.source: Typical NHS trust leaflets (headache 10–30% with standard needles)

points: Discomfort, infection (more the longer it stays), bleeding or trauma, rarely a false passage.

pitfalls: Listing only benefits and glossing over serious risks.
Not mentioning alternatives / the option of no treatment.
Failing to assess capacity or check understanding.
Consenting for a procedure beyond your competence (should escalate).

cognition.summary: Screen cognition with a named tool, decide between **delirium** and **dementia** (or both), and look for reversible causes. A collateral history is essential.

sections.title: Tools
items: **AMTS** (10 items; a score under 8 suggests impairment): age, time to the nearest hour, an address to recall at the end, year, place, recognise two people, date of birth, the year WW1 or WW2 started, the monarch, count down from 20 to 1
**4AT** for delirium: alertness, AMT4, attention (months backwards), acute change or fluctuation; **4 or more = likely delirium**
Fuller tools: MoCA, ACE-III (memory clinic)

sections.title: Delirium or dementia
items: Delirium: acute onset, fluctuating, **inattention**, altered consciousness
Dementia: gradual, progressive, attention preserved early

sections.title: Look for causes
items: Infection, drugs (anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines), retention, constipation, pain, dehydration, hypoxia, electrolytes
Bloods: FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, LFT, TFT, B12 and folate; CT head if indicated

tips: Name the tool and the score.
Get a collateral history.
Delirium is a medical emergency: treat the cause.

shoulder-exam.summary: Look → feel → move (active/passive) → special tests for the rotator cuff and impingement.

sections.title: Look
items: Front, side and behind: wasting (deltoid, supra/infraspinatus), asymmetry, scars, winging of the scapula

sections.title: Feel
items: Temperature; palpate the sternoclavicular joint, clavicle, AC joint, acromion, greater tuberosity, spine of scapula

sections.title: Move
items: Active then passive: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, internal/external rotation; note a **painful arc** (60–120° = impingement)

sections.title: Special tests
items: Supraspinatus (empty-can/Jobe), infraspinatus (resisted ER), subscapularis (Gerber lift-off)
Impingement (Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Weakness on empty-can test, inability to initiate abduction
Global restriction of active AND passive movement
Loss of external rotation + OA changes

tips: A painful arc 60–120° suggests subacromial impingement.
Restricted **passive** movement points to a frozen shoulder (not just a cuff tear).
Always examine the neck — cervical pathology refers to the shoulder.

genetic-hx.summary: Draw a three-generation pedigree, identify the likely pattern of inheritance, and talk about what it means for the patient and their relatives.

sections.title: Drawing
items: Square = male, circle = female, diamond = unknown; filled = affected; a line through = deceased
Double line = consanguinity; arrow = the proband
Ages, diagnoses and ages at diagnosis or death; ethnicity

sections.title: Patterns
items: Autosomal dominant: every generation, both sexes, male-to-male transmission
Autosomal recessive: siblings affected, unaffected parents, consanguinity
X-linked recessive: affected males, carrier females, no male-to-male transmission

sections.title: Counselling
items: Implications for relatives; consent for testing; confidentiality; referral to clinical genetics

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Cystic fibrosis, counselling a parent** (came up 2023 and often before): autosomal recessive; two carrier parents have a **1 in 4** chance of an affected child each pregnancy (1 in 2 carrier); found on the newborn blood spot, confirmed with a sweat test; what it means day to day, and testing for siblings and future pregnancies

tips: Male-to-male transmission rules out X-linked.

explain-med.summary: Explain a new medication so the patient can take it safely — what it’s for, how to take it, key side effects and safety-critical points, and monitoring. Tailor to the drug’s must-know message.

sections.title: Set up
items: Confirm identity; check what they know about the medication and why it’s being started
Check allergies and current medications (interactions)

sections.title: Explain the drug
items: What it’s for and how it helps
How and when to take it (dose, route, timing, with/without food)
Common side effects and what to do about them
The **safety-critical point** for that drug (e.g. methotrexate weekly, warfarin INR, steroid don’t-stop, statin muscle pain)

sections.title: Safety-net & check
items: Monitoring/blood tests required; when to seek help
Check understanding (teach-back); offer written information (patient leaflet)

knowledge.about: Vitamin K antagonist: AF, DVT/PE, mechanical valves
points: What it does: makes the blood take longer to clot, to prevent a stroke or a clot.
How to take: once a day at the same time (usually 6pm), so the dose can change after a blood test. Tablets are coloured by strength (white 0.5 mg, brown 1 mg, blue 3 mg, pink 5 mg).
Monitoring: the INR, often weekly at first, then up to every 12 weeks once steady; most targets are 2.5 (range 2–3). Doses go in the yellow book.
Get help urgently: blood in the urine or stool, black stools, vomiting or coughing blood, a severe headache, a nosebleed over 10 minutes, and **any head injury** (go to A&E).

Interactions: many. Antibiotics (clarithromycin, erythromycin, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, co-trimoxazole), fluconazole and amiodarone raise the INR; aspirin and NSAIDs add bleeding; St John's wort and carbamazepine lower it. Tell every prescriber, pharmacist and dentist; ask before anything over the counter.
Diet and alcohol: keep vitamin K steady rather than avoiding it (leafy greens); no binge drinking; avoid cranberry and grapefruit juice.
Practical: carry the anticoagulant alert card. Teratogenic: reliable contraception, and plan any pregnancy (switch to heparin).

knowledge.about: AF stroke prevention, DVT/PE; not for mechanical valves
points: How to take: apixaban and dabigatran twice a day; rivaroxaban and edoxaban once a day (rivaroxaban 15/20 mg with food). Same times each day.
Missed dose: take it as soon as remembered the same day, then carry on; never double up.
Monitoring: no INR. Kidney function and a blood count before starting, then yearly; more often if kidney function is reduced (about every 3–6 months), or if frail or over 75.
Get help urgently: the same bleeding signs as warfarin, and any head injury (A&E).
Interactions: fewer than warfarin, but avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless prescribed; some antiepileptics, antifungals and HIV drugs interact.
Practical: alert card; tell the dentist and anyone planning a procedure (it may be paused). Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
The rule that matters: **once a week**, on the same day each week. Never daily: a daily dose can be fatal. Only one tablet strength (2.5 mg).
Folic acid: 5 mg once a week on a different day from the methotrexate, to cut side effects.
Takes 6–12 weeks to work.
Monitoring: FBC, U&E and LFT every 2 weeks until on a stable dose for 6 weeks, then monthly for 3 months, then every 12 weeks; results in the monitoring booklet.
Get help urgently: sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, unexplained bruising or bleeding (bone marrow); new cough or breathlessness (pneumonitis); jaundice or abdominal pain (liver).
Avoid: trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (marrow toxicity); NSAIDs only with advice; live vaccines (flu jab and pneumococcal are fine and recommended). Keep alcohol well within 14 units.

Pregnancy: teratogenic. Women: reliable contraception during and for 6 months after stopping; men: 3 months after (the product licence), though rheumatology may continue low-dose methotrexate in men planning a family (BSR 2022).
Infection: tell the team; it may be paused.
knowledge.source: BSR DMARD monitoring guideline; BSR 2022 (prescribing in pregnancy); BNF (methotrexate)

knowledge.about: Type 1, or type 2 when other treatment is not enough
points: Injecting: abdomen or thighs, rotating sites (lumps from one spot change absorption); a new needle each time; hold for 10 seconds.

Hypos: below 4 mmol/L ("four is the floor"): shaky, sweaty, hungry, confused. 15–20 g of fast sugar (5–7 glucose tablets, or 150–200 ml of pure fruit juice), recheck after 10–15 minutes, repeat up to 3 times if still low, then a starchy snack.
Sick days: never stop the insulin; check glucose more often (and ketones in type 1); keep drinking; seek help if vomiting.

Driving: tell the DVLA. Check glucose within 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving; don't drive at 5 or below ("five to drive"); keep sugar in the car; if hypo, stop, treat, and wait 45 minutes after glucose is back above 5.
Storage: spares in the fridge; the pen in use at room temperature for up to 4 weeks.
Alcohol: raises the hypo risk, including the next morning: eat with it.
knowledge.source: JBDS hypoglycaemia algorithm; DVLA INF294 (insulin and driving)

points: What it does: helps the body use its own insulin; doesn't cause hypos on its own; weight-neutral.
How to take: with or just after meals; started low and increased over weeks. Nausea and diarrhoea are common at first and usually settle (slow-release helps).
Sick-day rule: stop it if vomiting, with diarrhoea or unable to drink (risk of AKI and lactic acidosis); restart once eating and drinking for 24–48 hours.
Monitoring: kidney function (review the dose below eGFR 45, stop below 30); B12 can fall over years.
Practical: it may be paused around iodinated contrast if kidney function is poor.
How to take: every morning on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast or coffee; 4 hours apart from iron, calcium and antacids.

Monitoring: TSH every 3 months until it's stable (2 similar results in range, 3 months apart), then once a year; after a very high TSH it can take up to 6 months to settle. Feeling better takes weeks.
Too much: palpitations, tremor, weight loss, feeling hot, sleeplessness: report them.
Practical: free prescriptions (medical exemption certificate). Tell the team in pregnancy: the dose usually goes up straight away.

How to take: 70 mg **once a week**, first thing, on an empty stomach, swallowed whole with a full glass of plain tap water; stay upright for 30 minutes; nothing else to eat, drink or take for 30 minutes.
Stop and seek advice: new heartburn, pain on swallowing (oesophagitis); new thigh or groin pain (atypical fracture); jaw pain or a loose tooth.
Jaw: a dental check before starting, good oral hygiene, and tell the dentist.
Alongside: calcium and vitamin D, at a different time of day. Reviewed after about 5 years (a drug holiday may follow).
How to take: in the morning, with food.
Longer courses: after more than 3 weeks (or over 40 mg a day for more than a week), never stop suddenly (the adrenals have stopped making cortisol): it's tapered.
Steroid emergency card: for 5 mg prednisolone a day (or equivalent) for 4 weeks or more, or over 40 mg a day for more than a week; extra doses in a febrile illness, as advised.

Side effects: appetite and weight, high glucose, mood change and poor sleep, indigestion, infections, BP, thin skin and bruising; long term, osteoporosis (bone protection at 3 months or more, especially at 65+) and cataracts.
Infection: seek advice after contact with chickenpox or shingles if not immune; no live vaccines on high doses.
knowledge.source: NHS England National Patient Safety Alert NatPSA/2020/005 (steroid emergency card); BNF (corticosteroids)

knowledge.about: Cholesterol: cuts heart attack and stroke risk
points: How to take: atorvastatin at any time of day (simvastatin at night).
Side effects: report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, especially with dark urine (rare myositis).
Monitoring: LFTs before, within 3 months and at 12 months; lipids at 3 months, aiming for a fall of more than 40% in non-HDL cholesterol.
Interactions: no large amounts of grapefruit juice; clarithromycin means pausing it.
Pregnancy: stop beforehand.

knowledge.about: BP, heart failure, after an MI, kidneys in diabetes
points: How to take: started low; the first dose can make you dizzy, so it's often taken at bedtime.
Side effects: a dry cough in about 1 in 10 (switch to an ARB); rarely angioedema: swelling of the lips, tongue or face is an emergency.
Monitoring: kidney function and potassium before, 1–2 weeks after starting, and after each dose increase.
Sick-day rule: pause if vomiting, with diarrhoea or dehydrated.
Avoid: NSAIDs, potassium supplements and salt substitutes. Not in pregnancy.
Expect: 2–4 weeks before it helps (anxiety can feel worse at first), the full effect by 6–8 weeks; continue for at least 6 months after feeling better.
Not addictive, but don't stop suddenly: it's reduced slowly (discontinuation symptoms).

Side effects: nausea, headache, sleep change, sexual problems; in the first weeks, agitation or suicidal thoughts (especially under 25): tell someone straight away. Review within 2 weeks, or after 1 week if aged 18–25 or at risk of suicide.
Interactions: bleeding risk with NSAIDs, aspirin and anticoagulants; low sodium in older people; serotonin syndrome with tramadol, St John's wort and some others. Avoid alcohol.
The risk: about 1 in 10 babies exposed in pregnancy have a major malformation, and up to 4 in 10 have developmental problems.
The rule: not for anyone who could become pregnant unless on the Pregnancy Prevention Programme: highly effective contraception, and a signed annual risk form with a specialist.
Since 2024: not started in anyone under 55, men included, unless two specialists independently agree there's no other effective option (or the reproductive risks don't apply).
If they become pregnant: don't stop it suddenly (seizures); urgent review.

knowledge.about: Regular slow-release, with immediate-release for breakthrough pain
points: How to take: the slow-release dose twice a day, regularly; the immediate-release when pain breaks through (about a sixth of the daily dose); keep a note of how often.
Always: a laxative (constipation doesn't wear off). Nausea and drowsiness in the first week usually settle.
Too much: very drowsy, confused, jerking, hallucinations, pinpoint pupils: call for help.
Fears to address: addiction isn't a concern used for pain; it doesn't mean the end; the dose can be adjusted.
Driving: an offence if impaired; once stable many can drive, but not when starting or after a dose change.
knowledge.source: NICE CG140 (strong opioids in palliative care); the breakthrough fraction from EAPC

points: When: at least 2–4 weeks after a flare has settled (or during one, if flares are frequent); daily, usually lifelong.

Expect: flares can increase early on, so colchicine is offered alongside while the target is reached (a low-dose NSAID or steroid if colchicine isn't suitable). A low dose, raised monthly by urate level, until urate is below 360 (below 300 with tophi or ongoing flares).
Stop and seek help: any rash (rare severe reactions).
Interactions: azathioprine (dangerous together). Drink plenty of fluid.

pitfalls: Omitting the one safety-critical counselling point for the drug.
Not checking allergies/interactions before counselling.
No teach-back / understanding check.
Overwhelming with every side effect instead of the important ones.

falls-hx.summary: A “falls” history is really about the cause of the collapse (cardiac, neurological, mechanical) plus the multifactorial risk assessment in the older patient. Get a before/during/after account.

sections.title: Before
items: What were you doing? Warning symptoms (palpitations, chest pain, dizziness, aura)? Standing up (postural)? Provoking factors?

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis)**: Any warning? On exertion? Palpitations or chest pain first? Anyone in the family die suddenly young?
**Seizure**: Did you bite your tongue, wet yourself, jerk? Confused afterwards?
**Head injury on a blood thinner**: Did you hit your head? Are you on a blood thinner?
**Long lie and hip fracture**: Could you get up? How long were you on the floor? Can you bear weight?
**Stroke or TIA**: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, face drooping?
**Hypoglycaemia**: Diabetic, on insulin or a sulfonylurea? Any warning: sweaty, shaky, hungry?
**Upper GI bleed**: Vomited blood or coffee grounds? Black, tarry stools? On NSAIDs, steroids or blood thinners? Alcohol or liver disease?

sections.title: During
items: Witnessed? Loss of consciousness? Duration? Colour, jerking, tongue-biting, incontinence (seizure vs syncope)? Injury?

sections.title: After
items: Recovery time, confusion afterwards (post-ictal), residual symptoms

sections.title: Risk assessment (older patient)
items: Medications (antihypertensives, sedatives, polypharmacy), vision, cognition, continence, alcohol, previous falls, home hazards, gait/balance, footwear

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Osteoporosis** (came up 2024, with counselling): fragility fractures (from standing height or less), **steroids**, early menopause, low BMI, smoking, alcohol, a parent's hip fracture, RA; then FRAX or QFracture and DEXA, and how to take a bisphosphonate (empty stomach, upright for 30 minutes, a full glass of water)

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Sudden, no warning, palpitations/chest pain, quick recovery
Provoked (standing/pain/emotion), prodrome, quick recovery lying flat
On standing, on antihypertensives, drop in BP
Aura, jerking, tongue-biting, incontinence, prolonged post-ictal confusion

redflags: Syncope without warning (cardiac — risk of sudden death)
tips: Get a **witness** account — it’s the most useful part.
Tongue-biting, incontinence and post-ictal confusion point to a seizure over syncope.
In older patients do a multifactorial falls risk assessment (meds, vision, gait, home).

bls.summary: Adult basic life support with an AED (Resuscitation Council UK 2021). It's a performance station: do each step in order, out loud, with good compressions and minimal pauses.

sections.title: Safe, response, help
items: Check for danger; shake the shoulders gently and ask loudly “Are you alright?”
Shout for help

sections.title: Airway and breathing
items: Open the airway: head tilt–chin lift
Look, listen and feel for **normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds**. Occasional gasps (agonal breathing) are not normal breathing

sections.title: Call
items: Not breathing normally: call **999** (hospital: **2222**, arrest team) and ask for an **AED**; phone on speaker

sections.title: CPR
items: **30 compressions**: centre of the chest (lower half of the sternum), **5–6 cm** deep, **100–120 a minute**, full recoil between
Then **2 rescue breaths** (about 1 second each, chest rising) if trained; otherwise continuous compressions
Continue **30:2**; swap compressors every 2 minutes

sections.title: AED
items: As soon as it arrives: switch on and follow the prompts
Pads: below the right clavicle, and the left mid-axillary line (V6 position)
Everyone clear for the analysis and the shock; **restart compressions immediately** after it, for 2 minutes

sections.title: Keep going until
items: Qualified help takes over, the patient shows signs of life (waking, moving, opening eyes, breathing normally), or you're exhausted

pairs.title: If the station moves into hospital (ALS)
rows: Shock, 2 min CPR; adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock
Adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access, then every 3–5 min
4 Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia (metabolic), hypothermia · 4 Ts: thrombosis, tamponade, toxins, tension pneumothorax

tips: Narrate every step — the examiner marks what they hear.
Agonal gasps → start CPR.
Hands-only CPR is fine if you can't or won't give breaths.
Keep pauses short: compressions are what keep the brain alive.

cse-paper-c.summary: Write a safe, legal, unambiguous prescription — an inpatient drug chart from a guideline and BNF excerpts, or discharge medicines (a TTO) — as an FY1 would. 20 minutes, BNF allowed.

sections.title: Before writing
items: Patient details on every sheet: name, DOB, hospital number, address, ward
**Allergies** (and the reaction) first — then weight and renal/hepatic function
Read the guideline or the notes for what to continue, stop or change, and why

sections.title: Every prescription
items: **Generic** name, dose, route, frequency, start date; duration for antibiotics and short courses
No abbreviations for units or micrograms; legible; signed, dated, bleep
PRN: the indication, the dose, the minimum interval and the **maximum in 24 hours**
Don't forget: VTE prophylaxis, regular medicines, analgesia, laxatives with opioids, anti-emetics

sections.title: Controlled drugs (TTO)
items: Drug, **form**, **strength**, dose, and the **total quantity in words and figures** (“56 (fifty-six) 30 mg capsules”)
Patient name and address; prescriber signature and date; valid for 28 days

sections.title: Syringe driver (CSCI over 24 h)
items: Each drug, its dose over 24 hours, the diluent (usually water for injection) and the volume; the start time
Breakthrough doses prescribed separately as PRN (often about a sixth of the 24-hour opioid dose)

tips: Check allergies before anything else — a prescription for an allergen is a critical error.
Write “units” and “micrograms” in full.
Laxative with every regular opioid.

lifestyle.summary: A new diagnosis of diabetes, asthma, epilepsy or hypertension is not bad news in the SPIKES sense — it is a **handover of self-management**. The marks are in what the patient will do differently tomorrow.

sections.title: Establish the starting point
items: What do they already know or believe about the condition? Correct specific misconceptions rather than lecturing generally.
Ideas, concerns, expectations — “What worries you most about having this?”

sections.title: Explain in their terms
items: What the condition is, in one plain sentence with no jargon.
What it means for them specifically — work, driving, pregnancy, sport, alcohol.

sections.title: Hand over the management
items: What they do: monitoring, inhaler or injection technique, when to step treatment up.
What we do: reviews, monitoring bloods, screening for complications.
Red flags: exactly what would make them seek help, and who to contact.

sections.title: Close
items: Written information and the relevant patient organisation.
Check understanding by asking them to say the plan back.

points: Cardiac rehabilitation: strongly recommended (exercise, education, support).

Medicines: aspirin plus ticagrelor or prasugrel (usually 12 months), a high-dose statin, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker; GTN for chest pain (sit, spray, repeat after 5 minutes; 999 if the pain lasts 5 minutes after the second).
Driving (car): 1 week after successful angioplasty with good heart function, otherwise 4 weeks; no need to tell the DVLA. Lorry and bus drivers must.

Sex: once they feel well enough, and can walk briskly up two flights of stairs without chest pain or breathlessness. Work: often 4–6 weeks (10–12 for heavy manual work). Flying: often 3–10 days after an uncomplicated heart attack.
knowledge.source: DVLA (cardiovascular); BHF; NHS trust cardiac rehab advice

points: Structured education (DESMOND); weight loss, and remission is possible with a low-calorie diet.
Targets and checks: HbA1c about 48 (53 on drugs that cause hypos); yearly eye screening, feet, kidneys, BP and cholesterol.
Driving: only tell the DVLA if on insulin, or with a hypo risk that affects driving.
Free prescriptions if on diabetes medicines; sick-day rules for metformin.

pitfalls: Delivering a lecture on pathophysiology instead of a plan.
Omitting the practical consequences — driving, work, pregnancy — which are what the patient actually asked about internally.
No red flags and no safety net.
Not checking understanding, so a misconception goes home with them.

ng-tube.summary: Pass a tube into the stomach through the nose and throat for feeding, drug administration or draining stomach contents; know how to confirm correct placement.

sections.title: Why
items: The **only** GMC skill first taught in **final year**, and target level is **simulation-only** — a high-attention/new skill. The safety-critical step is **confirming gastric placement** before using the tube: a misplaced tube in the lung and then fed is a Never Event.

sections.title: Indications
items: Enteral feeding (unsafe swallow)
Drug administration
Gastric decompression/drainage (e.g. bowel obstruction — Ryle’s tube)

sections.title: Equipment
items: NG tube (fine-bore for feeding; wider Ryle’s for drainage)
Lubricant, glass of water & straw
pH indicator paper, catheter-tip syringe
Tape/securement, drainage bag/feed

sections.title: Prepare & measure
items: Consent; sit the patient upright
Measure **NEX**: from the tip of the **N**ose to the ear**E**lobe to the **X**iphisternum — note the marking

sections.title: Insert
items: Lubricate the tip; insert into a patent nostril, advancing along the floor of the nose
As it reaches the pharynx, ask the patient to sip water and swallow while you advance to the measured mark
Secure the tube to the nose/cheek

sections.title: Confirm position (safety)
items: Aspirate gastric contents; test on pH paper — **pH < 5.5 confirms gastric placement**
If unable to aspirate / pH not confirmatory / on acid-suppression: obtain a **chest X-ray** (gold standard) and get it interpreted
NEVER use the discredited “whoosh” auscultation test
Do **not** feed or give drugs until placement is confirmed

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Gastric aspirate pH **1–5.5** confirms placement (safe to use); pH >5.5 → do not use, recheck/CXR
Chest X-ray is the gold-standard confirmation when aspirate cannot be obtained or pH is inconclusive
Auscultation (“whoosh” test) is discredited — never use it to confirm

tips: **pH 1–5.5 = safe to use**; if in doubt, CXR — this is the marked safety point.
Measure NEX before inserting.
Never auscultate to confirm; never feed until confirmed.

otoscopy.summary: Perform basic otoscopy and identify common abnormalities.

sections.title: Why
items: Examination of the external canal and tympanic membrane, often paired with **hearing tests** (whisper test + Rinne & Weber tuning-fork tests). GMC-required. **No dedicated Southampton resource folder was archived** — a materials gap (likely taught within ENT/clinical-skills teaching).

sections.title: Indications
items: Otalgia (ear pain)
Otorrhoea (discharge)
Hearing loss
Suspected foreign body / wax

sections.title: Equipment
items: Otoscope (working light)
Disposable specula — choose the **largest** that comfortably fits
512 Hz tuning fork (for Rinne & Weber)

sections.title: Otoscopy
items: Inspect the pinna and around the ear first (skin, mastoid)
Examine the *normal* (or less symptomatic) ear first
Pull the pinna **up and back** in adults (**down and back** in young children) to straighten the canal
Hold the otoscope like a pen, bracing your hand against the cheek to avoid trauma if the patient moves
Inspect the canal (wax, discharge, otitis externa) then the tympanic membrane

sections.title: Identify the TM
items: Normal TM: pearly-grey, translucent, cone of light antero-inferiorly, handle of malleus
Acute otitis media: red/bulging TM, loss of light reflex
Effusion (glue ear): dull TM ± fluid level/bubbles
Perforation; cholesteatoma (attic crust)

sections.title: Hearing tests
items: Whisper test: mask the other ear (rub the tragus), whisper a number ~60 cm away and ask them to repeat it
Weber: strike a **512 Hz** fork, place on the forehead midline — lateralises **to** the affected ear in conductive loss, **away** from it in sensorineural loss
Rinne: fork on mastoid (bone) then at the meatus (air) — **air > bone = normal (“Rinne positive”)**; bone > air suggests conductive loss

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Use a **512 Hz** tuning fork for Rinne & Weber (mid-range — audible yet decays slowly)
Weber lateralises **to** the affected ear = conductive; **away** = sensorineural. Rinne: air>bone = normal

tips: Bracing hand + “largest speculum that fits” = key safety/technique marks.
Pinna direction differs in children — say it.
Interpret Weber + Rinne **together** — never one alone.

abg-interp.summary: Oxygenation first, then pH, then which component explains it, then compensation — and the anion gap in a metabolic acidosis.

sections.title: Order
items: PaO₂ against the FiO₂ (expect PaO₂ ≈ FiO₂% − 10, in kPa); <8 kPa = respiratory failure
pH: acidaemia <7.35, alkalaemia >7.45
PaCO₂ (respiratory) and HCO₃⁻/base excess (metabolic): which one matches the pH?
Compensation; anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃), normal about 10–14

pairs.title: Patterns
rows: Low PaO₂, normal or low CO₂

tips: Say the order before reading the numbers.

ll-neuro.summary: The same inspect → tone → power → reflexes → sensation → coordination → gait sequence for the legs. Gait and Romberg add localising value.

sections.title: Inspection
items: Wasting, fasciculations, scars, deformity, walking aids

sections.title: Tone
items: Roll the leg, lift the knee (spasticity), test for clonus at the ankle

sections.title: Power
items: Hip flexion (L1/2), knee ext (L3/4)/flexion (L5/S1), ankle dorsiflexion (L4/5)/plantarflexion (S1/2), MRC 0–5

sections.title: Reflexes
items: Knee (L3/4), ankle (S1/2), plantar — **up-going (Babinski) = UMN**

sections.title: Sensation
items: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, proprioception by dermatome

sections.title: Coordination & gait
items: Heel-to-shin; observe gait (spastic, ataxic, high-stepping, waddling); **Romberg’s** test (sensory ataxia)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Increased tone, clonus, brisk reflexes, up-going plantars
Upper motor neurone lesion (e.g. cord compression)
Broad-based, unsteady gait, no worse with the eyes closed (Romberg negative)
Bilateral spastic weakness with a sensory level
Spinal cord compression — a surgical emergency

tips: An up-going plantar (Babinski) is a hard UMN sign — check it.
A **sensory level** with bilateral leg weakness = cord compression until proven otherwise.
Romberg tests proprioception (dorsal columns), not the cerebellum.

uro-hx.summary: Separate storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia) from voiding (hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling) symptoms, and screen the red flags — haematuria, retention and infection.

sections.title: Storage symptoms
items: Frequency, urgency, nocturia, urge incontinence

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Retention**: Can you pass urine at all? Painful, swollen lower tummy?
**Cancer (bladder, prostate)**: Blood in the urine? Bone pain, weight loss?
**Cauda equina**: Numb between the legs or around the bottom? Any change in your bladder, bowels or sexual function? Both legs?
**Urosepsis**: Fever, shivers, pain in the side or back?

sections.title: Voiding symptoms
items: Hesitancy, poor/intermittent stream, straining, incomplete emptying, terminal dribbling

sections.title: Red-flag & context screen
items: **Visible haematuria** (bladder cancer), dysuria/fever (UTI/pyelonephritis), acute retention (can’t pass urine, suprapubic pain)
Weight loss, bone pain (metastatic prostate); fluid intake, caffeine; medications

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **Nephrotic syndrome** (came up 2025, with U&E and a urine dip): **frothy urine**, swelling (puffy eyes in the morning, ankles later), weight gain, recent infection, NSAIDs, autoimmune symptoms, diabetes. The triad: heavy proteinuria, low albumin, oedema; ask about clots (VTE risk) and infections

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Older man, voiding symptoms, enlarged smooth prostate
Dysuria, frequency, urgency, cloudy urine ± fever
Visible haematuria, weight loss, irregular hard prostate
Urgency, frequency, urge incontinence, no obstruction
Sudden inability to void, painful palpable bladder

redflags: Aged 45+ with unexplained visible haematuria (no UTI, or persisting after treating one) → suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)
Weight loss / bone pain (metastatic prostate cancer)
tips: Split symptoms into **storage vs voiding** — it points to the cause.
Painless visible haematuria at 45+ is a suspected cancer referral (bladder or kidney) until proven otherwise (NICE NG12).
Always ask about acute retention — a can’t-miss emergency.

cough-hx.summary: Duration separates acute (usually infective) from chronic cough, and the associated symptoms point to the cause. Always screen for the red flags of malignancy and TB.

sections.title: Characterise
items: Duration (acute <3 wk vs chronic >8 wk), dry vs productive, sputum colour/volume, **haemoptysis**, diurnal/nocturnal, triggers

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Lung cancer**: Coughing blood? Weight loss? A hoarse voice? Do you or did you smoke?
**TB**: Night sweats, weight loss? Contact with TB, time in a country where it's common?
**PE**: Sudden breathlessness? Sharp pain breathing in? Coughed blood? A swollen calf? A long journey, surgery or being immobile, the pill or HRT, cancer, a clot before?
**Pneumonia with sepsis**: Fever, shivers, confusion, breathless at rest?
**Heart failure**: How many pillows do you sleep on? Ever woken up gasping? Ankles swollen by the evening?

sections.title: Associated
items: Breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain, fever, weight loss, night sweats, reflux, postnasal drip, ACE-inhibitor use

sections.title: Red-flag screen
items: Haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats (malignancy/TB), smoking pack-years, TB contacts/travel, occupational exposure

sections.title: Variants that have come up in finals
items: **TB** (came up 2025, with a chest X-ray): cough over 3 weeks, **night sweats, weight loss, haemoptysis**; born in or travel to a high-incidence country, contacts, HIV, homelessness, prison, alcohol. Then sputum for AFB, the X-ray, isolation, and contact tracing

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Chronic cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, smoker
Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss, contacts/travel
Chronic dry cough, reflux symptoms, drug history

redflags: Aged 40+ and ever smoked, with an unexplained cough → chest X-ray within 2 weeks; unexplained haemoptysis at 40+ → suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12)
tips: Duration is the first discriminator: acute infective vs chronic.
Always ask about haemoptysis, weight loss and night sweats (cancer/TB).
A persistent cough on an ACE inhibitor is a common, easily-missed cause.

msk-hx.summary: Which joints, how they started, and whether the pattern is **inflammatory** or **mechanical** — then function and the hot joint that can't be missed.

sections.title: The joints
items: Which joints: one, a few, many; small or large; symmetrical
Onset, pattern over time; swelling, redness, locking, giving way

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Septic arthritis**: One hot, swollen joint you can barely move? Fever? A joint replacement?
**Compartment syndrome**: After an injury or a cast: pain out of proportion, worse on stretching, tight?
**Malignancy**: Pain at night or at rest? Weight loss? Ever had cancer?
**Giant cell arteritis**: Over 50 with a new headache: tender scalp, jaw pain when chewing, any change in vision?

sections.title: Inflammatory or mechanical
items: Inflammatory: morning stiffness over 30–60 min, better with use
Mechanical: worse with use, short stiffness, end of day

sections.title: Function and systemic
items: Dressing, stairs, work, hobbies
Fever, weight loss, rash, eyes, bowel, urethritis; psoriasis, IBD, gout; diuretics

sections.title: Injury
items: Mechanism; able to weight-bear (Ottawa rules); numbness or weakness

redflags: Hot, swollen joint: **septic arthritis** until aspirated (aspirate before antibiotics)
tips: Ask about function: it drives management.
One hot joint = aspirate.

cse-child-dev.summary: From a developmental assessment, record what the child was **observed** doing and what was **reported**, domain by domain, with the age each milestone fits, then give a developmental age per domain and overall.

sections.title: Open with the context
items: Who assessed, who was present, birth history (term, delivery, weight, any SCBU), general health, how the child engaged

sections.title: Four domains, each the same way
items: **Gross motor**, **fine motor and vision**, **hearing, speech and language**, **social and self-care**
Under each: **observed** (with the age), **reported** (with the age), and **not yet observed or reported** (the next milestone, with its age)
“Domain assessment: 9–12 months”

sections.title: Close
items: Overall developmental age and whether it matches the chronological age (corrected if premature)
Any concern: a limit age missed, or a domain lagging

pairs.title: Anchors around a year
rows: Pincer grip, object permanence, responds to name, “dada” babble
Walks alone, first words, drinks from a beaker

tips: Split observed from reported — the model answer does, every domain.
Give the age next to every milestone.
Write the “not yet” line: it is what places the upper bound.

bowel-hx.summary: Characterise the change, distinguish acute (usually infective) from chronic, and screen the lower-GI cancer and IBD red flags. Ask specifically about blood and weight loss.

sections.title: Characterise
items: Frequency & consistency (Bristol), duration (acute <2 wk vs chronic), nocturnal symptoms, urgency, tenesmus, mucus

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Colorectal cancer**: Blood mixed in? Weight loss, tiredness? Family history? Over 50?
**Bowel obstruction**: Vomiting? Have your bowels or wind stopped? Swollen tummy, colicky pain? Previous surgery or a hernia?
**Severe colitis**: How many times a day, at night, with blood? Fever, tummy pain?
**Dehydration and AKI**: Keeping fluids down? Passing urine? Dizzy on standing?
**C. difficile**: Antibiotics or a hospital stay recently?

sections.title: Red-flag screen
items: **Rectal bleeding / blood mixed in stool**, unintentional **weight loss**, iron-deficiency anaemia symptoms, family history of bowel cancer/IBD
Abdominal/back pain, mass

sections.title: Context
items: Recent travel, contacts, antibiotics (C. diff), diet, alcohol; systemic (fever); thyroid symptoms; medications

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss, iron deficiency — **FIT test first**: FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g, or a rectal or abdominal mass → suspected cancer pathway (NICE DG56/NG12)
Chronic bloody diarrhoea, urgency, systemic features, young patient
Chronic, no red flags, related to stress, relieved by defecation

redflags: Rectal bleeding / blood mixed in the stool
New change in bowel habit over 50 / abdominal or rectal mass
tips: Explicitly ask about **blood in the stool and weight loss** — the key cancer red flags.
Acute vs chronic is the first split (infective vs structural/inflammatory).
Don’t diagnose IBS in the presence of any red flag — investigate first.

iv-infusion.summary: Set up and run through an intravenous infusion; be aware of the different equipment and devices used.

sections.title: Why
items: Prime the line, exclude air, connect to a patent cannula, and set an accurate rate against the prescription.

sections.title: Indications
items: IV fluid resuscitation/maintenance
IV medication administration

sections.title: Equipment
items: Prescribed fluid bag
Giving set (± volumetric pump)
Patent IV cannula, flush
Drip stand

sections.title: Prepare
items: Check the prescription and the fluid bag against it (right fluid, additives, expiry, no cloudiness)
Close the roller clamp; spike the bag; hang it

sections.title: Prime
items: Squeeze the drip chamber to half-fill it
Open the roller clamp and run fluid through the whole line to **exclude all air**, then close
Confirm the cannula is patent (flushes without pain/swelling)

sections.title: Run
items: Connect to the cannula using ANTT
Set the rate — via a pump, or by drops/min (drops/min = volume(mL) × drop factor ÷ time(min))
Label the bag/line; monitor the site and the patient

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Drip rate (drops/min) = volume(mL) × drop factor ÷ time(min). Standard giving set = **20 drops/mL** (blood set = 15)
Routine maintenance fluids ≈ **25–30 mL/kg/day** water, with ~1 mmol/kg/day Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ and 50–100 g/day glucose

tips: Exclude **all air** from the line — a safety marker.
Right-check the prescription and the bag before connecting.
Be able to calculate a manual drip rate.

bloods.summary: Read FBC, U&E and LFTs as patterns, not single numbers — and act on the dangerous ones first (potassium, AKI).

sections.title: FBC
items: Hb low: look at the **MCV** — microcytic (<80: iron deficiency, thalassaemia), normocytic, macrocytic (>100: B12 or folate, alcohol, liver, hypothyroid, drugs)
WCC and differential; platelets

sections.title: U&E
items: **AKI** (KDIGO): creatinine up ≥26.5 µmol/L in 48 hours, or ≥1.5× baseline in 7 days, or urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
High urea : creatinine ratio: dehydration or an upper GI bleed

sections.title: LFT
items: Hepatitic (ALT/AST high) or cholestatic (ALP, GGT, bilirubin high); AST:ALT >2 suggests alcohol

pairs.title: Hyperkalaemia (UK Kidney Association 2020)
rows: **30 mL 10% calcium gluconate IV** (if ECG changes)
10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose IV; salbutamol nebulised as an adjunct
Find the cause; remove potassium (stop drugs, treat AKI)

tips: Compare with the previous results.
Act on the dangerous number first.

capacity.summary: The Mental Capacity Act 2005: presume capacity, assess it for **this decision**, support the person to decide, and if they lack it, act in their best interests.

sections.title: Principles
items: Presume capacity; help them decide; an unwise decision isn't incapacity; best interests; least restrictive option

sections.title: The test
items: Is there an impairment of the mind or brain?
Can they **understand**, **retain**, **weigh** and **communicate** the decision?

sections.title: If they lack capacity
items: Best interests: their wishes and values; consult an LPA for health and welfare, family, or an IMCA if no one
A valid advance decision refusing treatment must be respected

sections.title: Document
items: The decision, the test, your reasons

sections.title: Tips
items: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.
An advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed, and say “even if life is at risk”.

safeguarding.summary: Listen, believe, do not investigate. Your job is to hear it, keep them safe, record it verbatim and refer — and to be honest that you cannot promise secrecy.

sections.title: Create the conditions
items: See the person ALONE. Never with the accompanying adult or partner present.
Unhurried, private, and say you have time.

sections.title: Listen
items: Open questions only. Let them tell it. Do not interrogate, do not fill gaps, do not ask leading questions — it can compromise a later investigation.

sections.title: Be honest about confidentiality
items: Do not promise secrecy. Explain, early and plainly, that if someone is at risk you will have to share with people whose job is to keep them safe.

sections.title: Act
items: Immediate safety first. Record verbatim, in their words, with a body map for injuries.
Refer to the safeguarding lead the same day. In children, the named doctor or nurse.
Ask about others at risk — children in the household, dependants.

points: Children: physical, emotional, sexual, neglect. Adults also: financial, domestic, discriminatory, organisational, self-neglect, modern slavery.
knowledge.source: Care Act 2014; Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023)

points: Never promise to keep it secret: explain who you'll need to tell, and why.
Tell the safeguarding lead and follow local procedure (children's social care); the police if anyone is in immediate danger.
FGM in under-18s: if you see it or are told, a mandatory duty to report to the police.
Adults with capacity: usually their consent to share, unless others (children) are at risk or there's a serious crime.
Document their words verbatim; don't investigate or ask leading questions yourself.
knowledge.source: Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023); FGM Act 2003 s5B (mandatory reporting); GMC confidentiality

pitfalls: Promising confidentiality you cannot keep — it destroys trust when you break it.
Asking leading or closed questions, which can taint evidence.
Interviewing rather than listening. You are not the investigator.
Paraphrasing instead of recording their exact words.
Forgetting other people in the household.
Seeing them with the suspected perpetrator present.

explain-proc.summary: Distinct from consent: here the task is comprehension, not authorisation. Structure it as before, during, after — and say what it will feel like, which is what patients actually want to know.

sections.title: Check the starting point
items: What have they been told, and what do they want to know?

sections.title: Why
items: What question the test answers, and what we would do differently with the result.

sections.title: Before
items: Preparation — fasting, bowel prep, stopping anticoagulation, arranging an escort.

sections.title: During
items: Where, how long, who will be there, sedation or anaesthetic.
What it will FEEL like — the part patients care about and clinicians skip.

sections.title: After
items: Recovery, driving, work, when and how results come, and who to contact if something is wrong.

sections.title: Close
items: Check understanding, invite questions, offer written information.

points: Why: to drain the bladder (retention, measuring output, after surgery).
How: a soft tube through the urethra into the bladder, with numbing gel; a small balloon holds it in. A few minutes; uncomfortable rather than painful.
After: a bag; drink plenty; report fever, pain or blood; how long it will stay.
Before: nothing to eat for 6 hours (sips of water up to 2 hours).
During: a throat spray or sedation; a thin camera through the mouth into the stomach; 5–10 minutes; biopsies don't hurt.
After: sore throat; with sedation, someone to take them home and no driving for 24 hours.
Before: a low-residue diet for a couple of days, bowel prep (laxatives) the day before; stop iron tablets a week before.
During: sedation or gas and air; a camera through the back passage around the large bowel; 30–45 minutes; polyps can be removed.
After: wind and bloating; with sedation, as for an OGD; report pain, fever or heavy bleeding.
knowledge.source: UK colonoscopy quality standards (Rees et al., Gut 2016); NHS trust leaflets

points: A cannula; the dye gives a warm feeling, and a feeling of having wet yourself (you haven't); a few minutes in an open ring.
Checks: kidney function, allergies, metformin, pregnancy.
knowledge.source: Royal College of Radiologists; NHS patient information

points: A long tube, loud noises (headphones), 20–60 minutes; keeping still matters.
Checks: pacemakers, metal implants or fragments (welders' eyes), claustrophobia; no ionising radiation.
An ultrasound of the heart: gel and a probe on the chest, lying on the left side; 30–45 minutes; no radiation. (A TOE, through the throat, is different.)
Curled on the side or sitting forward; local anaesthetic; a thin needle between the bones of the lower back to take a little fluid; 20–30 minutes.
After: a headache in some (fluids, simple painkillers; tell us if severe); rare bleeding or infection.
knowledge.source: Typical NHS trust leaflets (headache 10–30% with standard needles)

pitfalls: Explaining the mechanism and omitting the experience.
Forgetting the practicalities — escort, fasting, time off work.
Not saying how and when results will arrive, which is the commonest source of later complaints.
Using “scope”, “NBM”, “cannula” without translation.

growth.summary: Plot accurately on the UK-WHO chart, correct for prematurity, and recognise when a child is crossing centiles.

sections.title: Plotting
items: Right chart for sex; dot at the exact age; **correct for gestation** if born before 37 weeks, until age 2
Weight, length or height, head circumference; mid-parental height for context

pairs.title: Concern (NICE NG75)
rows: If birthweight was below the 9th centile
If birthweight was between the 9th and 91st

tips: Always correct for prematurity.

chest-pain-hx.summary: The priority is to separate the immediately life-threatening causes (ACS, PE, aortic dissection) from benign ones. Characterise the pain (SOCRATES) and screen the killers.

sections.title: Characterise (SOCRATES)
items: Site, Onset (sudden/exertional), Character (crushing/tearing/pleuritic), Radiation (jaw/arm/back), Associated (sweating, nausea, breathlessness), Timing, Exacerbating/relieving (exertion, GTN, movement, food), Severity

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **ACS**: Heavy or crushing? Spreading to the jaw or arm? Sweaty, sick, worse on exertion?
**PE**: Sudden breathlessness? Sharp pain breathing in? Coughed blood? A swollen calf? A long journey, surgery or being immobile, the pill or HRT, cancer, a clot before?
**Aortic dissection**: Did it come on suddenly, tearing, through to the back?
**Pneumothorax**: Sudden, sharp pain on one side? Tall and thin, or asthma or COPD?
**Oesophageal rupture**: Did it start after forceful vomiting?

sections.title: Screen the killers
items: ACS: central/crushing, radiates to jaw/arm, sweating, nausea, worse on exertion
PE: pleuritic, breathless, haemoptysis, calf pain, recent immobility/surgery
Dissection: sudden **tearing** pain radiating to the back, unequal
Also GORD, musculoskeletal, pericarditis, pneumonia

sections.title: Risk factors
items: Cardiac: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, family history
VTE: recent surgery/immobility, malignancy, COCP, prior DVT/PE

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Central crushing pain, radiates to jaw/arm, sweating, worse on exertion
Pleuritic, breathless, tachycardic, VTE risk factors
Sudden tearing pain to the back, unequal BP/pulses
Sharp, worse lying flat, better sitting forward, recent viral illness
Related to food/posture or reproducible on palpation

tips: Actively exclude the three killers (ACS, PE, dissection) in every chest-pain history.
Ask about VTE risk factors — easily forgotten and exam-relevant.
Offer an ECG and troponin as your immediate next steps.

cse-referral.summary: A letter from what you watched or read that tells the receiving team, in the first lines, **who the patient is, what you're asking, and how urgently** — then only the information they need.

sections.title: Layout
items: Your details and the recipient's (department, consultant), date
Patient name, DOB, NHS number, address
**Reason for referral** and the **urgency** (e.g. suspected cancer pathway) in the opening sentence
HPC — the relevant positives and negatives
Examination and investigation results
PMH, drugs, **allergies**, social situation that affects care
What you have already done or started, and your **specific question**
Signature, name, role, contact

tips: If the reader only reads the first two lines, they should know what you want.
Select: a referral is not a full history.
Normal values are provided — flag the abnormal ones.

contraception.summary: Find what matters to her, explain the options by effectiveness, check medical eligibility (**UKMEC**), and teach the method properly — including what to do when it goes wrong.

sections.title: Options
items: **LARC** (most effective, >99%): implant, IUS, copper IUD, injection
Pills: combined (COCP) and progestogen-only (POP); about 91% with typical use
Condoms: the only protection against STIs

sections.title: COCP: UKMEC 4 (don't use)
items: Migraine with aura; age 35+ smoking 15+ a day; BP ≥160/100; current or past VTE; current breast cancer; under 6 weeks postpartum and breastfeeding

sections.title: Missed pills (COCP)
items: One missed: take it now, carry on, no extra precautions
Two or more: take the last one now, condoms for 7 days; emergency contraception if in week 1 after unprotected sex

sections.title: Emergency contraception
items: **Copper IUD**: most effective, up to 5 days after UPSI (or after the earliest likely ovulation)
Ulipristal: up to 120 hours
Levonorgestrel: up to 72 hours (double dose if BMI >26 or weight >70 kg)

sections.title: Under 16
items: Fraser guidelines; safeguarding

sections.title: Tips
items: Ask what she wants from contraception before recommending.
POP: traditional 3-hour window; desogestrel 12 hours.

venous-exam.summary: Examine standing: the distribution of the varicosities, the skin changes of chronic venous insufficiency, and the ulcer. Duplex scanning has replaced most bedside tests.

sections.title: Inspect (standing)
items: Varicosities: great saphenous (medial leg and thigh) or small saphenous (posterior calf)
Skin: oedema, haemosiderin staining, venous eczema, **lipodermatosclerosis**, atrophie blanche
Ulcers: **gaiter area**, often above the medial malleolus — shallow, sloping edges

sections.title: Palpate
items: Temperature; tenderness or a hard cord (thrombophlebitis)
Cough impulse at the **saphenofemoral junction** (2–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle)

sections.title: Complete
items: **Duplex ultrasound** (reflux and its level)
**ABPI** before compression (compression is safe at ABPI ≥0.8)
Arterial and abdominal examination

tips: Arterial ulcers: punched-out, painful, at pressure points; venous: gaiter area, shallow.
Mention ABPI before compression — a safety point.

resp-hx.summary: Breathlessness spans cardiac, respiratory and other causes. Time course, associated symptoms and the cardiac/respiratory screen point to the diagnosis.

sections.title: Characterise
items: Onset (sudden vs gradual), duration, exertional tolerance (how far can you walk?), diurnal variation, positional (orthopnoea, PND)

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Heart failure**: How many pillows do you sleep on? Ever woken up gasping? Ankles swollen by the evening?
**PE**: Sudden breathlessness? Sharp pain breathing in? Coughed blood? A swollen calf? A long journey, surgery or being immobile, the pill or HRT, cancer, a clot before?
**Pneumothorax**: Sudden, sharp pain on one side? Tall and thin, or asthma or COPD?
**ACS**: Heavy or crushing? Spreading to the jaw or arm? Sweaty, sick, worse on exertion?
**Severe asthma or anaphylaxis**: Can you finish a sentence? Wheeze? Lips or tongue swelling, a new food or drug?
**Lung cancer**: Coughing blood? Weight loss? A hoarse voice? Do you or did you smoke?

sections.title: Associated symptoms
items: Cough, sputum, haemoptysis, wheeze, chest pain, fever
Cardiac: orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, palpitations

sections.title: Screen causes
items: Asthma/COPD: wheeze, triggers, smoking, diurnal
Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, oedema
PE: sudden onset, pleuritic, VTE risk
Pneumonia: fever, productive cough; anaemia; anxiety

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Wheeze, known diagnosis, triggers, smoking history
Orthopnoea, PND, ankle oedema, cardiac history
Sudden onset, pleuritic pain, VTE risk factors
Gradual, fatigue, pallor, no chest signs

tips: Quantify with exercise tolerance and orthopnoea (how many pillows).
Separate cardiac (orthopnoea/PND/oedema) from respiratory (wheeze/cough/sputum) early.
Always screen for PE risk factors in acute breathlessness.

ul-neuro.summary: Inspection → tone → power → reflexes → sensation → coordination. The distribution of weakness (pyramidal, root, nerve) plus the reflex/tone pattern separates UMN from LMN.

sections.title: Inspection
items: Wasting, fasciculations, tremor, posture (pronator drift), scars

sections.title: Tone
items: Assess at wrist and elbow — spasticity (UMN), rigidity, or flaccidity (LMN)

sections.title: Power
items: Test shoulder abduction (C5), elbow flexion (C5/6)/extension (C7), wrist ext (C6/7), finger ext (C7), finger flexion (C8), finger abduction (T1), grade **MRC 0–5**

sections.title: Reflexes
items: Biceps (C5/6), supinator (C6), triceps (C7) — brisk (UMN) or absent/reduced (LMN)

sections.title: Sensation
items: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, proprioception — map by dermatome/nerve territory

sections.title: Coordination
items: Finger-to-nose (past-pointing/intention tremor), dysdiadochokinesia

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Increased tone, brisk reflexes, pronator drift, pyramidal weakness
Wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone, absent reflexes
Wasting + fasciculations AND brisk reflexes (mixed UMN/LMN)
Loss of pain/temperature with preserved proprioception

tips: Pronator drift is a sensitive early sign of a pyramidal (UMN) lesion.
Fasciculations + brisk reflexes together should make you think MND.
Grade power with the MRC scale (0–5), not vague terms.

palp-hx.summary: Characterise the awareness of the heartbeat and screen for a dangerous arrhythmia. The pattern (regular/irregular, fast/slow) and associated syncope guide urgency.

sections.title: Characterise
items: Ask them to **tap out** the rhythm — regular or irregular? fast or slow?
Onset/offset (sudden vs gradual), duration, frequency, triggers (caffeine, alcohol, exertion, stress)

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Ventricular arrhythmia**: Have you fainted or nearly? Chest pain or breathless with it? Known heart disease?
**Inherited heart disease**: Has anyone in the family died suddenly under 40?
**AF and stroke**: Is it irregular? Any weakness, numbness or trouble speaking?
**Thyrotoxicosis**: Weight loss, heat intolerance, shaky hands?
**Drugs**: Stimulants, caffeine, alcohol? Any medicine that lengthens the QT?

sections.title: Associated / red flags
items: **Syncope or pre-syncope**, chest pain, breathlessness (suggest a significant arrhythmia)
Family history of sudden cardiac death

sections.title: Causes to screen
items: Thyrotoxicosis (heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor), anaemia, anxiety, drugs (salbutamol, stimulants), alcohol, caffeine

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Sudden-onset regular fast palpitations, terminates abruptly
Structural heart disease, syncope, chest pain — dangerous
Weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, sweating

redflags: Palpitations with syncope (arrhythmia — risk of sudden death)
Family history of sudden cardiac death
tips: Ask the patient to tap out the rhythm — regular vs irregular is the key discriminator.
Palpitations + syncope = get an ECG and think dangerous arrhythmia.
Screen for thyrotoxicosis in every palpitations history.

sbar.summary: A performance station in disguise. Use **SBAR** and state the ask explicitly — the commonest failure is giving a narrative and leaving the listener to work out what you want.

sections.title: Prepare before dialling
items: Notes, observations, bloods and imaging in front of you. Know the drug chart and the resuscitation status.
Decide what you are asking for: advice, review, or acceptance of care.

sections.title: S — Situation
items: Who you are, where you are, who the patient is, and in one sentence why you are calling.

sections.title: B — Background
items: Presenting problem, relevant history, what has been done so far.

sections.title: A — Assessment
items: Your observations and your interpretation. Commit to an impression — “I think this is…”.

sections.title: R — Recommendation
items: The explicit ask, with a timeframe. Then confirm what was agreed and by whom.

sections.title: Close the loop
items: Document the call, the name of the person, and the plan. Escalate if you remain concerned.

pitfalls: Giving Situation and Background then stopping, so the senior must interview you.
No impression — “I do not know what is going on” without saying what you have considered.
Not stating a timeframe, so “I will come later” goes unchallenged.
Accepting a refusal you are still worried about, instead of escalating.
Not documenting the call.

cultures.summary: Take samples of peripheral venous blood to test for the growth of infectious organisms.

sections.title: Why
items: Aseptic non-touch technique (**ANTT**) is everything — contamination causes false positives, unnecessary antibiotics and prolonged admissions. Take **before** antibiotics wherever possible (Sepsis Six).

sections.title: Indications
items: Suspected bacteraemia / sepsis
Pyrexia of unknown origin
Suspected infective endocarditis (multiple sets from different sites)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Aerobic + anaerobic culture bottles
ANTT pack, 2% chlorhexidine/70% alcohol wipes
Needle & holder / winged collection set
Sharps bin

sections.title: Prepare (ANTT)
items: Wash hands, apron/gloves; assemble sterile field
Palpate and select the vein, then clean the skin for 30 seconds and let it dry fully — do **not** re-palpate afterwards
Clean the bottle tops and let dry

sections.title: Collect
items: Take blood (typically 8–10 mL per bottle for optimal yield)
Inoculate the bottles without changing the needle; avoid introducing air into the anaerobic bottle
Label at the bedside with time and site

sections.title: After
items: Dispose of sharps immediately; document; send promptly to the lab
For endocarditis: **3 sets from separate venepuncture sites**, ideally spaced

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Fill each bottle with **8–10 mL** blood — under-filling reduces sensitivity; inoculate aerobic then anaerobic
Infective endocarditis: **3 sets** from separate venepuncture sites, ideally spaced over time
Take **before** antibiotics where possible — but never delay antibiotics in septic shock

tips: ANTT + “don’t re-palpate after cleaning” is the single biggest marks source.
Correct **fill volume** (8–10 mL) matters for yield — don’t under-fill.
Before antibiotics; 3 sets for endocarditis.

obs-news.summary: Measure and record temperature, respiratory rate, pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturations and urine output.

sections.title: Why
items: The foundation of recognising the deteriorating patient. Six parameters feed **NEWS2** — respiratory rate, SpO₂, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness/new confusion (ACVPU) and temperature — uplifted by 2 for supplemental oxygen. Accurate obs, correctly recorded and *escalated*, are the first link in every acute chain.

sections.title: Indications
items: Routine monitoring of every inpatient
Assessing an acutely unwell or deteriorating patient
Baseline before/after a procedure, drug or transfusion
Triage and track-and-trigger (NEWS2)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Tympanic/oral thermometer
Manual or automated sphygmomanometer + correct-size cuff
Pulse oximeter (SpO₂ probe)
Watch with a second hand
NEWS2 observation chart

sections.title: Prepare
items: Wash hands, introduce yourself, confirm patient identity and gain consent
Ensure the patient is rested and comfortable

sections.title: Measure
items: Respiratory rate — count for a full 60 seconds while appearing to take the pulse (so it stays unconscious/accurate)
Oxygen saturations — probe on a warm finger; note if on air or O₂ (and how much)
Pulse — rate, rhythm and character for 60 seconds
Blood pressure — correct cuff at heart level; note lying/standing if postural symptoms
Temperature
Level of consciousness — ACVPU (Alert / Confusion (new) / Voice / Pain / Unresponsive)

sections.title: After
items: Document each value on the NEWS2 chart and calculate the aggregate score
Escalate per the NEWS2 threshold (e.g. NEWS ≥5 = urgent senior review)
Repeat at a frequency matched to the score/clinical concern

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: NEWS2 escalation: aggregate **≥5** = urgent response; **3 in any single parameter** = urgent ward-based review; **≥7** = emergency, consider critical care
Add **2** to the score for any supplemental oxygen; use SpO₂ Scale 2 (target 88–92%) for hypercapnic-risk patients

tips: Respiratory rate is the **most sensitive** early sign of deterioration — and the one most often fudged. Count it properly.
A NEWS2 of 3 in a *single* parameter still triggers review — not just the aggregate.
Add 2 to NEWS2 for any supplemental oxygen.
State your escalation plan out loud (who you’d call and when) — examiners reward safety-netting.

cse-mse.summary: Watch a psychiatric or GP consultation and **document the MSE, justifying each finding** from what you saw. Marked separately for written communication (headings, flow, succinctness), observations, and **interpretation** — a formulation of the likely diagnosis.

sections.title: Headings, in order
items: **Appearance and behaviour** — age, dress, self-care, eye contact, psychomotor (e.g. fidgeting with a ring), startle
**Speech** — rate, rhythm, tone, volume, quantity (pressured but interruptible?)
**Mood** (subjective, in their words: “worried”) and **affect** (objective: anxious, reactive, euthymic, flat)
**Thought** — form (racing, prolixity vs flight of ideas, loosening) and content (worries, overvalued ideas vs delusions, obsessions, **suicidal thoughts and protective factors**)
**Perception** — hallucinations (modality) vs illusions
**Cognition** — orientation to time, place, person; attention
**Insight** — do they recognise their worries as excessive?

sections.title: Justify and interpret
items: Each finding with its evidence: “pressured speech — she spoke rapidly and was hard to interrupt”
Use the terms precisely: an illusion is a misperception of something real; an overvalued idea isn't held with delusional intensity
End with a **formulation**: the most likely diagnosis and why, and risk

pairs.title: What separates the grades (from the commentary)
rows: No headings, missing important observations, no interpretation, or a “blunderbuss” verbatim record
Headings with the important observations under each, logical flow, succinct
All of that, plus the specific details (“icing on the cake”) and a reasoned formulation

tips: Write headings first, before the video starts, and fill them as you watch.
It is not a transcript: summarise and interpret.
Always document risk, even when it is low (“denied suicidal thoughts; husband a protective factor”).

mi-interview.summary: Very brief advice plus a **referral** beats a lecture every time. The mark is for eliciting motivation and offering a route, not for listing harms the patient already knows.

sections.title: Ask and assess
items: Ask permission to discuss it. Establish current use, previous attempts and what happened.
Assess readiness — importance and confidence, out of ten. The gap tells you where to work.

sections.title: Advise briefly
items: One sentence of personalised benefit, not a catalogue of risks.
Be explicit that the most effective route is support plus pharmacotherapy, not willpower.

sections.title: Act
items: Smoking: refer to the local stop-smoking service, offer NRT or varenicline. Very brief advice is Ask–Advise–Act.
Alcohol: score with AUDIT-C; offer brief intervention, and specialist referral where dependent — never abrupt cessation in dependence, because of withdrawal seizures.
Weight: agree one specific change; consider referral to a structured programme.

sections.title: Follow up
items: Book a specific review. Relapse is expected, not failure — say so before it happens.

points: Very brief advice: ask, advise ("the best thing you can do for your health"), act (refer).
Evidence: the NHS Stop Smoking Service roughly triples the chance of quitting compared with willpower alone.

Options: combination NRT (a patch plus a short-acting form), varenicline (a 12-week course, started 1–2 weeks before the quit date; nausea; back on the NHS as a generic since 2024), and vapes (far less harmful than smoking). Set a quit date.
Limit: 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days, with several drink-free days.
Units: a pint of 4% beer about 2.3; a 175 ml glass of 12% wine about 2.1; a bottle of wine about 9–10; a 25 ml spirit 1.
Screen: AUDIT-C (5 or more, then the full AUDIT).
Dependent drinkers mustn't stop suddenly (withdrawal seizures): medically supported detox.
knowledge.source: UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016); AUDIT-C

points: Losing 5–10% of body weight brings real benefits (BP, glucose, joints).
Activity: 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and strength work on 2 days.
Support: weight management services; GLP-1 medicines (semaglutide, tirzepatide) for some, through specialist services.
knowledge.source: UK CMO physical activity guidelines; NICE obesity guidance

pitfalls: Listing harms the patient can already recite — it produces resistance, not change.
Advising cessation with no referral and no pharmacotherapy, which achieves almost nothing.
Telling an alcohol-dependent patient to stop abruptly — withdrawal can kill.
Moralising, or using the word “should”.
Not asking permission first.

peak-flow.summary: Explain to a patient how to perform a peak expiratory flow, assess that it is performed adequately, and interpret the results.

sections.title: Why
items: A cheap, effort-dependent measure of large-airway obstruction — central to **asthma** diagnosis and monitoring. In an OSCE the *teaching* is the marked task: explain, demonstrate, check technique, then interpret.

sections.title: Indications
items: Diagnosis & monitoring of asthma (diurnal variability, response to treatment)
Assessing acute asthma severity
Monitoring COPD

sections.title: Equipment
items: Peak flow meter
Single-use disposable mouthpiece
Peak flow diary / predicted-value chart

sections.title: Teach & perform
items: Set the marker to zero and attach a clean mouthpiece
Stand up (or sit upright)
Take a maximal deep breath in
Form a tight seal around the mouthpiece with the lips
Blow out as hard and fast as possible — a short, sharp “huff”
Note the reading; repeat three times and record the **best** of three

sections.title: Interpret
items: Compare to the patient’s personal best or predicted (age/height/sex)
Acute asthma: 50–75% predicted = moderate, 33–50% = severe, <33% = life-threatening
Look for diurnal/day-to-day variability (>20% supports asthma)

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Acute asthma severity (% best/predicted PEF): moderate 50–75% · acute severe 33–50% · life-threatening <33%
Record the **best of three** technically-adequate attempts; diurnal variability >20% supports asthma

tips: It’s a **teaching** station — narrate each instruction and check the patient’s technique (common errors: not sealing lips, blowing slowly).
Best of **three**, not an average.
Always interpret against predicted/personal best — a raw number alone scores little.

cerebellar.summary: Screen for cerebellar dysfunction — the mnemonic **DANISH**: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Slurred (staccato) speech, Hypotonia/Heel-shin.

sections.title: Speech & eyes
items: Ask a phrase to elicit **staccato/scanning** dysarthria
Look for **nystagmus** (fast phase towards the lesion) on lateral gaze

sections.title: Upper limb
items: **Dysdiadochokinesia** (rapid alternating hands)
Finger-to-nose: **intention tremor** and past-pointing
Rebound phenomenon; tone (hypotonia)

sections.title: Lower limb & gait
items: Heel-to-shin ataxia
Gait: **broad-based, unsteady**, veering to the side of the lesion
