Romberg negative (distinguishes from sensory ataxia)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Ipsilateral limb signs (falls/points towards the lesion)
Truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, minimal limb signs

tips: Cerebellar signs are **ipsilateral** to the lesion.
Romberg is **negative** in cerebellar ataxia (positive = sensory).
Use DANISH so you don’t miss a component.

catheter.summary: Insert a urethral catheter in both male and female patients.

sections.title: Why
items: Aseptic insertion of a urethral catheter. Two absolute rules: **never inflate the balloon until urine flows**, and in males **replace the retracted foreskin** afterwards (to prevent paraphimosis).

sections.title: Indications
items: Acute urinary retention
Accurate urine-output monitoring (critically ill)
Bladder outlet obstruction; peri-operative; some incontinence

sections.title: Equipment
items: Catheter pack + sterile gloves
Catheter (12–16 Ch typical)
Anaesthetic lubricating gel
10 mL sterile water + syringe (balloon)
Drainage bag; ANTT

sections.title: Prepare
items: Consent; **offer a chaperone**; check allergies (e.g. latex); position (supine; female — legs abducted)
Establish a sterile field (ANTT); clean the meatus; drape

sections.title: Insert
items: Instil anaesthetic lubricating gel into the urethra (male: hold to allow it to work)
Male: insert to the **hilt** (to the bifurcation) before inflating. Female: advance until urine flows, then a further 2–3 cm
Confirm **urine flows**, then inflate the balloon with **10 mL sterile water**
Attach the drainage bag; secure

sections.title: After
items: **Replace the foreskin** in males
Document: indication, catheter type/size, residual volume, any difficulty (keep the batch label for the notes)
Note the residual (retention) volume

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Balloon: inflate with 10 mL sterile water — only once urine flows
Catheter size 12–16 Ch typical (larger for haematuria/clots)

tips: Never inflate the balloon until you see urine — inflating in the urethra causes serious trauma.
Insert to the hilt before inflating.
Replace the male foreskin afterwards — a commonly-forgotten safety step.

breast-exam.summary: Inspect (at rest and with manoeuvres) → palpate all quadrants + tail + nodes → characterise any lump. Always chaperoned; any discrete lump needs triple assessment (NICE NG12: aged 30+ with an unexplained lump → suspected cancer pathway).

sections.title: Inspect
items: At rest, arms raised, and hands pressing on hips: asymmetry, skin changes (**peau d’orange**, dimpling/tethering), nipple inversion/discharge, scars
Inspect both breasts in each position

sections.title: Palpate
items: Examine the normal breast first; palpate all four quadrants + the axillary tail of Spence with a flat hand
Characterise any lump: site, size, shape, consistency, mobility, tethering, tenderness
Examine the nipple; check for discharge

sections.title: Lymph nodes
items: Axillary nodes (support the arm), supraclavicular and infraclavicular nodes

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Hard, irregular, fixed/tethered lump ± skin dimpling ± nodes
Smooth, firm, highly mobile lump in a young woman

tips: Always use a **chaperone** and explain each step — professionalism marks.
Any discrete lump = triple assessment; don’t reassure without it. Aged 30+ with an unexplained lump: suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12).
Examine the normal side first for comparison.

sick-child.summary: Paediatric A to E with age-appropriate normal values, and the NICE fever **traffic light**. Shout early for the paediatric team.

sections.title: A to E
items: As in adults, with child-sized equipment and normal values for age
Glucose in every sick child ("Don't ever forget glucose")

sections.title: NICE fever traffic light — red features
items: Pale, mottled or blue; no response to social cues; weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
Grunting, RR >60, moderate or severe chest indrawing
Reduced skin turgor
Age **under 3 months with a temperature ≥38 °C**
Non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, status epilepticus, focal signs, bile-stained vomiting

tips: Under 3 months with a fever is red on its own.
Talk to the parent: they know when the child is different.

dvla.summary: The duty to notify is the **patient’s**. Yours is to tell them clearly, document it, and act if they will not — a station that is really about confidentiality and its limits.

sections.title: Know the rule
items: Common triggers: first unprovoked seizure (6 months off, car), epilepsy, syncope with injury or recurrence, TIA or stroke (1 month), arrhythmia causing incapacity, insulin-treated diabetes with impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, significant visual field loss, dementia.

After ACS a Group 1 (car) driver stops for 1 week if treated with successful PCI, otherwise 4 weeks, and need not notify the DVLA. Group 2 (bus/lorry) rules are much stricter. Check the DVLA guide rather than trusting memory.

sections.title: Tell the patient clearly
items: They must inform the DVLA and their insurer. Say it plainly, confirm they understood, and record that you said it.
Explain the consequences of not doing so — legal and insurance.

sections.title: If they will not
items: Explore why — work, income, independence, care responsibilities. Offer practical alternatives.
Explain that if they continue to drive you have a duty to inform the DVLA, and that you would tell them before doing so.
Involve a senior. Disclosure in the public interest is permitted and, if they continue driving, expected.

sections.title: Document
items: What you advised, that they understood, their response, and any disclosure and its justification.

points: First unprovoked seizure: 6 months off driving (12 if there's a cause that raises the risk). Epilepsy: 12 months seizure-free.
TIA or stroke: 1 month off; tell the DVLA if there are problems left after a month.
ACS: 1 week after successful angioplasty (good heart function), otherwise 4 weeks; no need to tell the DVLA. A pacemaker: 1 week.
Syncope: a simple faint, no restriction; unexplained, 6 months.
Diabetes on insulin: tell the DVLA; 2 or more severe hypos (needing help) while awake in 12 months means stopping; hypo awareness is required.
Vision: read a number plate at 20 metres.
knowledge.source: DVLA, Assessing fitness to drive (neurological, cardiovascular, diabetes, Appendix D)

points: Far stricter: for example, 10 years off all epilepsy medication and seizure-free for epilepsy; always tell the DVLA.
Telling the DVLA is the patient's legal duty; yours is to tell them clearly, and document it.
If they won't stop and keep driving: try to persuade them, tell them you'll inform the DVLA, then do so, and tell them you have (GMC).
knowledge.source: GMC confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive

pitfalls: Telling the patient you will inform the DVLA for them — the duty is theirs first.
Being vague, so they leave thinking it is a suggestion.
Not documenting the advice, which leaves you indefensible.
Disclosing without first telling the patient you intend to.
Forgetting the insurer, and forgetting Group 2 rules are different.

adherence.summary: Non-adherence is usually rational from where the patient is standing. Find the actual reason — cost, side effects, belief, complexity, or never having understood why — before doing anything else.

sections.title: Ask without judgement
items: Normalise first, then ask openly. “Most people miss doses — how often does it happen for you?”

sections.title: Find the reason
items: Intentional: side effects, beliefs about harm, feeling well, distrust, cost.
Unintentional: forgetting, complexity, dexterity, swallowing, packaging, chaotic circumstances.

sections.title: Address that reason specifically
items: Side effects: switch, reduce, or manage them — do not just reassure.
Beliefs: explore rather than contradict, then give the specific information that matters.
Complexity: simplify the regimen, once-daily where possible, dosette box, blister packs, reminders.

sections.title: Agree and review
items: A shared plan, one change at a time, with a review date. Respect an informed decision not to take it.

pitfalls: Asking “you are taking your tablets, aren’t you?” — which guarantees a yes.
Repeating why the drug is important without finding out why it is not being taken.
Dismissing a side effect the patient is genuinely experiencing.
Adding a drug to fix a problem caused by not taking the existing ones.
Treating an informed refusal as a failure to educate.

cse-rx-chart.summary: Write a safe, legal, unambiguous prescription — an inpatient drug chart from a guideline and BNF excerpts, or discharge medicines (a TTO) — as an FY1 would. 20 minutes, BNF allowed.

sections.title: Before writing
items: Patient details on every sheet: name, DOB, hospital number, address, ward
**Allergies** (and the reaction) first — then weight and renal/hepatic function
Read the guideline or the notes for what to continue, stop or change, and why

sections.title: Every prescription
items: **Generic** name, dose, route, frequency, start date; duration for antibiotics and short courses
No abbreviations for units or micrograms; legible; signed, dated, bleep
PRN: the indication, the dose, the minimum interval and the **maximum in 24 hours**
Don't forget: VTE prophylaxis, regular medicines, analgesia, laxatives with opioids, anti-emetics

sections.title: Controlled drugs (TTO)
items: Drug, **form**, **strength**, dose, and the **total quantity in words and figures** (“56 (fifty-six) 30 mg capsules”)
Patient name and address; prescriber signature and date; valid for 28 days

sections.title: Syringe driver (CSCI over 24 h)
items: Each drug, its dose over 24 hours, the diluent (usually water for injection) and the volume; the start time
Breakthrough doses prescribed separately as PRN (often about a sixth of the 24-hour opioid dose)

tips: Check allergies before anything else — a prescription for an allergen is a critical error.
Write “units” and “micrograms” in full.
Laxative with every regular opioid.

drug-hx.summary: Every medicine, how it's actually taken, and every allergy with its reaction. The ones people forget are the ones that matter.

sections.title: What
items: Prescribed: name, dose, frequency, route, indication, how long, who prescribes
Over the counter, herbal, recreational
Often forgotten: inhalers, eye drops, patches, injections, contraception and HRT

sections.title: How
items: Recent changes; adherence (ask without judgement); who manages them (dosette, carers)

sections.title: Allergies
items: Drug and **the reaction**: allergy (rash, anaphylaxis) or intolerance (nausea)

sections.title: Sources
items: Patient, GP record or Summary Care Record, community pharmacy, their own medicines; reconcile within 24 hours of admission

tips: Always the reaction, not just the drug.
Ask “Any medicines you buy yourself?”

abg-take.summary: Insert a needle into a patient's radial artery to take a sample of arterial blood and interpret the results.

sections.title: Why
items: Both the *sampling* and the *interpretation* are examinable. Have a **systematic ABG approach** ready and know how to check collateral flow.

sections.title: Indications
items: Suspected respiratory failure / to assess oxygenation & ventilation
Acid–base disturbance (DKA, sepsis, renal failure)
Any critically unwell patient / rapid electrolyte & lactate

sections.title: Equipment
items: Pre-heparinised ABG syringe + needle
Antiseptic wipe, gauze
Local anaesthetic (optional)
Sharps bin; ice if delayed analysis

sections.title: Prepare
items: Confirm indication, consent; check collateral flow (Allen’s test)
Palpate the radial pulse at the wrist with the wrist slightly extended

sections.title: Sample
items: Clean the skin; insert the needle at 45–90° over the point of maximal pulsation, bevel up
Arterial blood pulsates and self-fills the pre-heparinised syringe
Withdraw and apply firm pressure for ≥5 minutes (longer if anticoagulated)
Expel any air bubbles, cap, and analyse promptly (on ice if >10 min)

sections.title: Interpret (systematic)
items: **Oxygenation:** PaO₂ vs FiO₂ (expect PaO₂ ≈ FiO₂% − 10 in kPa). <8 kPa on air = respiratory failure
**Type 1 resp failure** = hypoxaemia + normal/low CO₂ (V/Q mismatch); **Type 2** = hypoxaemia + high CO₂ (hypoventilation)
**pH:** acidaemia (<7.35) or alkalaemia (>7.45)
**Respiratory component:** PaCO₂ (raised → respiratory acidosis; low → respiratory alkalosis)
**Metabolic component:** HCO₃⁻ / base excess (low → metabolic acidosis; high → metabolic alkalosis)
Compensation, and the **anion gap** in a metabolic acidosis (raised: DKA/lactate/toxins; normal: GI/renal HCO₃⁻ loss)

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Normal ranges: pH 7.35–7.45 · PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa · PaO₂ 11–13 kPa (on air) · HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L · BE −2 to +2
Respiratory failure: PaO₂ <8 kPa. Type 1 = normal/low CO₂; Type 2 = PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa
Apply firm pressure ≥5 min post-sampling (longer if anticoagulated) — it’s an artery

tips: Allen’s test first — a classic marks item.
Firm pressure ≥5 min (arterial!).
Have a slick, systematic interpretation ready — state pH → resp → metabolic → compensation.

cbg.summary: Measure the concentration of glucose in the blood at the bedside; record and interpret the result.

sections.title: Why
items: A near-patient test that must be part of the workup of **every** reduced-consciousness or acutely unwell patient — “don’t ever forget glucose”.

sections.title: Indications
items: Diabetes monitoring
Reduced consciousness / collapse / seizure
Any acutely unwell patient

sections.title: Equipment
items: Glucometer + in-date, calibrated test strips
Single-use lancet
Alcohol wipe/gauze, sharps bin

sections.title: Prepare
items: Check the meter is calibrated and the strips are in date
Wash the patient’s hands (warm water improves flow); do not use alcohol on the sample finger (falsely alters result)

sections.title: Measure
items: Lance the **side** of a fingertip (less painful, more capillaries)
Apply a hanging drop to the strip; read the value
Dispose of the lancet in the sharps bin

sections.title: Interpret
items: Hypoglycaemia <4.0 mmol/L (“four is the floor”) → treat immediately
Confirm with a lab glucose if the result doesn’t fit the picture

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Hypoglycaemia = blood glucose **<4.0 mmol/L** (“four is the floor”)
Conscious/able to swallow: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck at 15 min; if unable: IM glucagon or IV 10% glucose

tips: Check strips **in date & calibrated** — an easy safety mark.
Side of the finger, not the pulp.
Know hypo management (“15 g fast carbs, recheck at 15 min”; IV glucose/IM glucagon if unable to swallow).

gals.summary: A rapid MSK screen to detect abnormality and decide which regional exam to do next. Three screening questions + look at Gait, Arms, Legs and Spine.

sections.title: Screening questions
items: Any pain or stiffness in muscles, joints or back?
Can you dress yourself completely without difficulty?
Can you walk up and down stairs without difficulty?

sections.title: Gait
items: Observe walking: symmetry, stride, arm swing, turning; smoothness of the phases of gait

sections.title: Arms
items: Hands out (palms down then up), make a fist, pincer grip, squeeze MCPs; hands behind head (shoulder) and behind back

sections.title: Legs
items: Inspect; passive knee flexion (feel for crepitus), patellar tap; internally rotate the hip; squeeze the MTPs; inspect the feet/soles

sections.title: Spine
items: Inspect from behind (scoliosis) and the side (kyphosis/lordosis); lateral neck flexion (ear to shoulder); “touch your toes” (lumbar flexion)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Prompts the relevant regional look/feel/move exam

tips: GALS is a **screen** — its job is to flag which regional exam to do, not to diagnose.
Record findings as a grid (appearance / movement per region).
The three questions have high sensitivity for significant MSK disease.

spine-exam.summary: Look, feel, move, then the special tests and a neurological screen. The point of the station is usually to show you'd catch the red flags.

sections.title: Look
items: From behind and the side: scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis, muscle wasting, scars, posture; gait

sections.title: Feel
items: Spinous processes and paraspinal muscles for tenderness; sacroiliac joints

sections.title: Move
items: Cervical: flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation
Thoracic: rotation (seated)
Lumbar: flexion (**Schober's test** — under 5 cm increase suggests restriction), extension, lateral flexion

sections.title: Special tests and neuro
items: **Straight leg raise** (sciatica, L4–S1; pain at 30–70°)
**Femoral stretch** (L2–L4)
Lower limb neurological examination

sections.title: Complete
items: Ask about cauda equina symptoms; examine perianal sensation and anal tone if suspected

tips: Always ask the cauda equina questions.
Reduced lumbar flexion in a young man with morning stiffness: think ankylosing spondylitis.

vasc-hx.summary: Separate claudication from rest pain and tissue loss, catch acute ischaemia, and take the cardiovascular risk factors.

sections.title: Claudication
items: Cramping calf, thigh or buttock pain on walking, relieved by rest within minutes; the distance
Buttock pain with erectile dysfunction: aortoiliac disease (Leriche)

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Acute limb ischaemia**: Did the leg suddenly go cold, pale, painful, numb or weak? An irregular heartbeat?
**Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia**: Pain at night, eased by hanging the leg out of bed? Ulcers, black toes?
**AAA**: Pain through to the back? Did you collapse or faint? A pulsing in the tummy? Over 65, a smoker, a known aneurysm?
**Infected diabetic foot**: Fever, spreading redness, a smell, a wound that won't heal?

sections.title: Critical limb-threatening ischaemia
items: Rest pain, worse at night, eased by hanging the leg over the bed
Ulcers or gangrene

sections.title: Acute ischaemia
items: Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia, paralysis (6 Ps)

sections.title: Risks
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, family history, other vascular disease (MI, stroke)

pairs.title: Differentials
rows: Leg pain on walking relieved by sitting or bending forward

tips: Ask how far they can walk.
Acute limb ischaemia is an emergency.

testicular.summary: Inspect standing and lying, palpate each testis, epididymis and cord, and answer the three questions about any lump: can you get above it, is it separate from the testis, does it transilluminate? **Chaperone.**

sections.title: Set up
items: Consent, chaperone, privacy; expose from umbilicus to knees; examine standing, then lying

sections.title: Inspect
items: Scrotal skin, swelling, asymmetry, position (a high-riding testis), scars; inguinal region

sections.title: Palpate
items: Each testis between thumb and two fingers: size, consistency, lumps, tenderness; normal side first
Epididymis (posterolateral) and the spermatic cord up to the external ring
Any lump: **can you get above it?** Separate from the testis? Cough impulse? **Transilluminate**

sections.title: Complete
items: Inguinal lymph nodes (scrotal skin drains here; the testis drains to the para-aortic nodes)
Hernia examination; abdominal examination

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: Can't get above it, cough impulse
Hydrocele (examine the testis: an underlying tumour?)
“Bag of worms”, worse standing, usually left
Varicocele (a new or right-sided one: think renal tumour)
Hard, painless lump in the testis
Testicular cancer: urgent USS, AFP, β-hCG, LDH; suspected cancer pathway
Sudden severe pain, high-riding, absent cremasteric reflex

tips: Examine the normal side first.
A teenager with sudden testicular pain has torsion until surgery says otherwise.
Professionalism and chaperone are marked.

interpreter.summary: A professional interpreter, not a family member, and you speak to the **patient** throughout. Doubling the time and halving the sentence length is most of the technique.

sections.title: Before
items: Book a professional interpreter — telephone or in person. Do not use a relative for anything clinical or sensitive; they filter, and they may be part of the problem.
Brief the interpreter: purpose, sensitivity, that you want a faithful translation rather than a summary.
Allow roughly double the time.

sections.title: During
items: Seat so you face the patient. Address the PATIENT in the second person, not the interpreter in the third.
Short sentences, one idea at a time, no idiom, no jargon, then pause.
Watch the patient’s face while the interpreter speaks — that is where the information is.

sections.title: Checking
items: Teach-back through the interpreter. Ask the patient to say the plan in their own words.
If a long exchange happens between interpreter and patient, ask what was said.

sections.title: After
items: Document that an interpreter was used, and which language. Offer written information in their language.

pitfalls: Using a family member — especially a child — for anything sensitive.
Speaking to the interpreter in the third person, which excludes the patient from their own consultation.
Long compound sentences and idiom.
Not documenting that an interpreter was used.
Assuming a nod means comprehension.

cse-handover.summary: Record every job from a handover, put them in order, and **justify the order**. The examiner marks the jobs captured, the prioritisation and its justification, and the clarity of what you wrote. A different order can still be excellent if your reasons are sound.

sections.title: While you watch
items: One line per patient: **name, DOB or hospital number, ward/bed, the job, why**
Capture the details you would need to act: results to chase, drugs, timings, who is waiting

sections.title: Prioritise
items: Sick before routine: **A, B, C** problems first (new breathlessness: think PE, ACS, pneumonia; new confusion: sepsis, metabolic, stroke)
Time-critical jobs others are waiting on can come first if quick (a cannula a CT scan is waiting for)
Routine jobs that cause no harm if done in two to four hours: NG tube, fluids, chasing bloods
Conversations with relatives: important, rarely urgent — can it be delegated, or a time agreed?

sections.title: For each job, say
items: Why it sits where it does
What you would do (assess, investigate, escalate) and whether someone else could do it
When you would escalate to your senior

tips: The justification is where the marks are: one clear reason per job.
Number the list; don't bury the order in prose.
Say what you would delegate and to whom.

uncertainty.summary: Telling someone you do not know what is wrong, without either alarming them or dismissing them. “Your tests are all normal” alone is heard as “I do not believe you”.

sections.title: Name it positively
items: Say what has been excluded and what that genuinely rules out — not just “normal”.
Say plainly that the symptoms are real and you believe them.

sections.title: Explain the uncertainty
items: Why tests can be normal in a real condition. What you think is most likely, and how confident you are.

sections.title: Make a plan anyway
items: Uncertainty is not the absence of a plan. Symptomatic management, a time course to expect, and a review point.

sections.title: Safety-net explicitly
items: Specific symptoms that mean come back sooner, who to contact, and by when. Then confirm they can repeat it.

pitfalls: “Everything is normal” with nothing after it — heard as disbelief.
Manufacturing a diagnosis to fill the silence.
“Come back if it gets worse” with no specifics and no owner.
Not saying you believe the symptoms are real.
Concealing uncertainty to appear competent.

injections.summary: Prepare and administer injectable drugs and prefilled syringes.

sections.title: Why
items: Right drug, right route, right technique. The pre-administration **checks** and correct site/angle are the marked elements. IM injections use the **Z-track technique** to lock the drug in the muscle and stop it tracking back into subcutaneous tissue.

sections.title: Indications
items: Vaccines & many drugs (IM/SC)
IV medications (via cannula)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Drug + diluent, syringe & needles (drawing-up + administration)
ANTT items, sharps bin, drug chart

sections.title: Check & prepare
items: Confirm the “five rights”: right patient, drug, dose, route, time (+ documentation & allergies)
Check drug name, dose, expiry; draw up; expel air; label if not immediate

sections.title: Administer — IM
items: Choose the site: **deltoid** (small volumes/vaccines), **vastus lateralis** (infants; self-administered adrenaline), **ventrogluteal** (larger volumes, avoids nerves/vessels)
Apply **Z-track** traction: pull the skin ~2–3 cm to one side with the non-dominant hand and hold it
Insert like a dart at **75–90°**, leaving ~⅓ of the shaft exposed. Aspiration is no longer advised for vaccines (Green Book); follow local policy for other drugs
Inject slowly — **~1 mL per 10 seconds**; wait ~10 s, withdraw, then release the traction (locks the drug in the muscle)

sections.title: Administer — SC / IV
items: SC: abdomen/outer thigh/upper arm; pinch the skin; insert at 45–90°
IV: via a patent cannula using ANTT; flush before and after
Dispose of the sharp immediately; document; monitor for reactions

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: IM injection: insert at **75–90°**, inject **~1 mL per 10 seconds**; Z-track technique prevents drug tracking back into subcutaneous tissue
Sites: deltoid ≤1 mL (vaccines) · ventrogluteal up to ~2.5–3 mL (larger volumes) · vastus lateralis (infants, EpiPen)

tips: State the pre-administration checks (five rights + allergies) — heavily marked.
Correct site & angle per route; **Z-track** for IM.
Never re-sheath; sharps straight to the bin.

oxygen.summary: Prescribe and administer oxygen safely using an appropriate delivery method; monitor and adjust as needed.

sections.title: Why
items: Oxygen is a **drug** — it must be prescribed with a **target saturation range** and titrated. The key safety issue is CO₂ retention in some COPD patients.

sections.title: Indications
items: Hypoxaemia (acute illness, peri-arrest, breathlessness)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Delivery device: nasal cannulae (1–4 L/min), simple face mask (5–10 L/min), non-rebreathe mask with reservoir (15 L/min), or Venturi (fixed FiO₂)

sections.title: Prescribe & deliver
items: Assess the patient and SpO₂; in an emergency give high-flow via a non-rebreathe mask at 15 L/min
Prescribe the **target range** and the device on the drug chart
For COPD/retainer risk: controlled O₂ via a Venturi (e.g. 24–28%), target 88–92%, check an ABG

sections.title: Monitor
items: Titrate to keep SpO₂ within the target range
Reassess with ABG if hypercapnia is a risk; wean as the patient improves

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Target SpO₂ **94–98%** for most; **88–92%** if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure
Devices: nasal cannulae 1–6 L/min · simple mask 5–10 L/min · non-rebreathe (reservoir) 15 L/min · Venturi = fixed FiO₂

tips: “Oxygen is a drug” — prescribe a **target range**, not just “O₂”.
Know the two target ranges (94–98% vs 88–92%).
Non-rebreathe 15 L/min for the acutely hypoxic; Venturi for controlled delivery.

life-change.summary: Breaking news that changes someone's life (an amputation, a stoma, a disability). The SPIKES structure, then the practical future: what life will look like, and who will help.

sections.title: Prepare
items: Know the facts: why, what the operation means, rehabilitation, prosthetics, prognosis
Private room, time, support person if wanted

sections.title: SPIKES
items: Perception, invitation, a warning shot, then the news in small chunks
Allow silence; respond to grief and anger

sections.title: The future
items: What daily life will be like: mobility, home, work, driving, identity
The team: physiotherapy, OT, prosthetics, psychology, peer support (e.g. the Limbless Association)

sections.title: Close
items: Their questions; written information; follow-up; who to contact

sections.title: Tips
items: Don't rush to the positives.
Ask what matters most to them.

parent-results.summary: Explaining a result or a diagnosis to a parent, and to the child, at the level each can use — honest, concrete, checked back.

sections.title: The parent
items: What they know and fear first; chunk and check; ICE
Avoid blame; give written information and who to call

sections.title: The child
items: Simple, concrete words; honest; include them, don't talk over them
Check understanding: ask them to tell you, or draw it
Adolescents: speak to them directly; Gillick competence for decisions

sections.title: Tips
items: Use the child's name.
Kneel or sit at their level.

milestones.summary: Four domains, a few anchor ages each, and the limit ages that mean refer.

sections.title: Gross motor
items: Head control ~4 months · sits unsupported ~7 months · crawls ~9 months · walks ~12 months · runs ~2 years · stairs alternating feet ~3–4 years

sections.title: Fine motor and vision
items: Reaches ~4–5 months · transfers hand to hand ~6 months · pincer grip ~9–12 months · tower of 2 bricks ~15 months · draws a circle ~3 years, a cross ~4 years

sections.title: Speech, language and hearing
items: Babbles ~6 months · first words ~12 months · 2-word phrases ~2 years · short sentences ~3 years

sections.title: Social
items: Social smile ~6 weeks · stranger anxiety ~8–9 months · waves bye-bye ~10–12 months · feeds with a spoon ~15–18 months

tips: The CSE child-development paper (Izzy) tests exactly this — practise it.

breast-hx.summary: Characterise the lump or symptom, ask about the nipple and the skin, and take the risk factors and family history. Most women are afraid of cancer: ask about that.

sections.title: The symptom
items: Lump: when noticed, size change, relation to the cycle, pain
Nipple: discharge (bloody? one duct?), inversion; skin changes; axillary lump

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Breast cancer**: Hard, fixed, growing? Skin dimpling, an inverted nipple, bloody discharge, a lump in the armpit?
**Inflammatory breast cancer**: Red, swollen, orange-peel skin without a fever?
**Spread**: Bone pain, breathlessness, headaches, weight loss?
**Abscess**: Hot, red, painful, with a fever? Breastfeeding?

sections.title: Risk factors
items: Age, family history (breast or ovarian cancer, BRCA), previous breast disease or chest radiation
Hormonal: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, HRT, COCP
Alcohol, obesity

sections.title: Ideas, concerns, expectations
items: Ask directly what they're worried it is

sections.title: Urgent referral (NICE NG12)
items: Aged 30+ with an unexplained breast lump — Suspected cancer pathway
Aged 50+ with one-sided nipple discharge, retraction or other concerning change — Suspected cancer pathway

tips: Every discrete lump needs triple assessment.
Ask about family history across both sides.

thyroid-hx.summary: Symptoms of thyroid status (hyper or hypo), the neck itself, and the eyes; then the background that points to a cause.

sections.title: Hyperthyroid
items: Weight loss with a good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, diarrhoea, light periods

sections.title: Screen the killers: straight after SOCRATES, as one block
items: **Airway compression**: Any trouble breathing or swallowing, noisy breathing, worse lying flat?
**Thyroid cancer**: Is the lump growing fast? A hoarse voice? Radiation to the neck in the past?
**Agranulocytosis on carbimazole**: On carbimazole or PTU: any sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever?
**Sight-threatening eye disease**: Blurred vision, colours looking washed out, double vision?
**Thyroid storm**: Fever, racing heart, agitation or confusion?

sections.title: Hypothyroid
items: Weight gain, cold intolerance, fatigue, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, heavy periods, low mood, hoarse voice

sections.title: Neck and eyes
items: Lump: onset, growth, pain (thyroiditis); compression: dysphagia, stridor, voice change
Eyes: grittiness, protrusion, double vision (Graves')

sections.title: Background
items: Autoimmune disease; **drugs** (amiodarone, lithium, levothyroxine, carbimazole); family history; pregnancy or recent delivery; neck radiation

redflags: Rapidly enlarging lump, hoarseness, stridor, lymph nodes (thyroid cancer)
Fever and sore throat on carbimazole (agranulocytosis — stop and check FBC)
tips: Ask about the eyes — Graves' is the only cause with eye disease.
Ask about amiodarone and lithium.

cse-gp-notes.summary: Document a GP consultation as a structured problem-based entry — and answer the short questions that follow (e.g. safe antihistamines in pregnancy, a differential).

sections.title: Structure
items: Header: consultation type (face to face, phone), patient, DOB, date, doctor

**Problem** (one line) → **HPC** (pertinent positives and negatives) → **PMH** → **DH** (and any changes made, with why) → **allergies** → **SH** → **examination** → **impression** → **plan** (including safety-netting and follow-up)

sections.title: Content that scores
items: Relevant negatives (no bleeding, no urinary symptoms)
Medicine changes made in the consultation (e.g. stopping fexofenadine in pregnancy, offering a better-studied antihistamine)
Safety-netting: what would make them come back, and when

tips: Answer the extra questions in full sentences, separately from the notes.
A problem-based layout is quicker to write and to mark than prose.

discharge.summary: Discharge planning starts on admission: medically fit, functionally safe, supported at home, with the right medicines and a clear plan for the GP.

sections.title: Checklist
items: Medically optimised; the MDT agrees (physiotherapy, OT, social work); equipment or package of care
TTOs reconciled; changes explained
Follow-up booked; district nurse; the **discharge summary** to the GP (diagnosis, medicine changes with reasons, actions for the GP)
The patient and carers understand the plan and the red flags; transport

tips: The CSE discharge summary paper practises the written half of this.

pain.summary: Assess the pain, treat it in steps with regular simple analgesia as the base, and prescribe the laxative with the opioid.

sections.title: Assess
items: SOCRATES, a pain score, its effect on function; neuropathic features

sections.title: The ladder
items: Step 1: paracetamol (1 g up to four times a day; reduce if under 50 kg or in liver disease) ± NSAID (caution: kidneys, GI, asthma, CVD; give a PPI)
Step 2: weak opioid (codeine)
Step 3: strong opioid (morphine); **laxative with every opioid**; anti-emetic if needed

sections.title: Special cases
items: Renal impairment: morphine accumulates — seek advice (e.g. oxycodone, alfentanil)
Neuropathic pain: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (NICE CG173)
Breakthrough opioid dose ≈ one sixth of the 24-hour regular dose (palliative care)

tips: Regular beats PRN for constant pain.

social-hx.summary: Who the patient is outside hospital, and what they'll need to go home: work, home, function, support, habits.

sections.title: Ask about
items: Occupation (and exposures); home: type, stairs, who lives there
Function: washing, dressing, cooking, shopping; mobility aids; carers or package of care
Driving; finances; dependants; support network
Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs; diet, exercise; travel; pets

tips: Link it to the plan: discharge starts here.

dre.summary: On a manikin in the OSCE. Consent and chaperone, left lateral position, inspect, then a gloved lubricated finger: tone, the rectal wall all round, the prostate, and the glove afterwards.

sections.title: Set up
items: Explain, consent, **chaperone**; left lateral, knees to chest; cover the patient

sections.title: Inspect
items: Skin tags, haemorrhoids, fissures, fistulae, warts, blood, prolapse

sections.title: Palpate
items: Lubricated gloved index finger, pad first, gently
**Anal tone**: ask them to squeeze
Rectal wall 360°: masses, tenderness
Men: **prostate** — size, consistency, surface, median sulcus, tenderness
On withdrawal: look at the glove (blood, melaena, mucus, stool colour)

sections.title: Finish
items: Clean the patient, allow them to dress; thank them; document with the chaperone's name

tips: Say what you'd look for on the glove.
Chaperone and dignity are where the marks are.

speculum.summary: On a manikin. Consent and chaperone, inspect the vulva, insert a warmed, lubricated speculum, visualise the cervix, take samples if needed, then the bimanual examination.

sections.title: Set up
items: Consent, **chaperone**, privacy, empty bladder; supine, heels together, knees apart; cover

sections.title: Speculum
items: Inspect the vulva
Warm, water-based lubricant; insert closed, then rotate the blades to horizontal and open gently
Inspect the cervix: ectropion, polyps, lesions, discharge; take swabs or a cervical screening sample
Partially close before withdrawing; inspect the vaginal walls on the way out

sections.title: Bimanual
items: Two fingers in the vagina, the other hand on the abdomen
Uterus: size, position (anteverted or retroverted), mobility, tenderness
Adnexae both sides; **cervical excitation** (PID, ectopic)

pairs.title: Signs that matter
rows: HPV-negative: 5-yearly (from July 2025, for ages 25–64; previously 3-yearly under 50) — check current NHS guidance

tips: Explain each step before you do it.
Professionalism carries the station.

obs-palp.summary: Antenatal: inspect, measure the symphysis–fundal height, find the lie, presentation and engagement, listen to the fetal heart. Postnatal: the 6–8 week check of mother as well as baby.

sections.title: Antenatal palpation
items: Consent, chaperone, semi-recumbent (left tilt if uncomfortable)
Inspect: distension, scars, striae, linea nigra
**Symphysis–fundal height** in cm ≈ weeks of gestation (±2 cm) from 24 weeks
**Lie** (longitudinal, transverse, oblique), **presentation** (cephalic, breech), **engagement** in fifths palpable
Fetal heart: Pinard or Doppler — normal **110–160** bpm

sections.title: Postnatal check
items: Mood (baby blues vs postnatal depression vs psychosis), BP, bleeding (lochia), perineum or wound
Feeding, contraception, pelvic floor, cervical screening if due

tips: Plot SFH on a customised chart.
Small for dates → growth scan.

paeds-bls.summary: Paediatric basic life support (RCUK 2021). Children arrest from hypoxia, so breaths come first: **5 rescue breaths**, then **15:2**.

sections.title: Safe, stimulate, shout
items: Check for danger; stimulate and ask “Are you alright?” (don't shake an infant); shout for help

sections.title: Airway and breathing
items: Infant: **neutral** head position; child: head tilt–chin lift
Look, listen, feel for normal breathing up to 10 seconds

sections.title: Breaths
items: **5 rescue breaths** — infant: mouth over mouth and nose; child: mouth to mouth, pinching the nose
Watch for chest rise; reposition if it doesn't

sections.title: Compressions
items: No signs of life: **15 compressions : 2 breaths**, 100–120 a minute
Depth at least **one third** of the chest (about 4 cm infant, 5 cm child)
Infant: two-thumb encircling technique (or two fingers); child: one or two hands, lower half of the sternum

sections.title: Call
items: Alone: call (speakerphone) straight away if you can; otherwise after about 1 minute of CPR
AED in children as for adults (paediatric pads if available)

tips: Breaths first — it's the difference from adult BLS.
Say your depth target as a third of the chest.

ct-head.summary: Fresh blood is bright (hyperdense). The shape tells you where it is; midline shift and hydrocephalus tell you how urgent.

sections.title: Read
items: Details; brain window; blood (hyperdense), CSF spaces, ventricles, midline shift, grey–white differentiation; bone window for fractures

pairs.title: Patterns
rows: Blood in the basal cisterns and sulci
Early hypodensity, loss of grey–white differentiation, hyperdense artery
CT within 1 hour after head injury (NICE NG232)
GCS <13 at first assessment or <15 at 2 hours, suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal deficit, more than one vomit

tips: Name the window you're looking at.

cse-discharge.summary: Tell the GP what happened, what changed, and **what they need to do** — the actions for the GP are the part that keeps the patient safe.

sections.title: Sections
items: Patient details; admission and discharge dates; ward; consultant
**Diagnosis** (primary and secondary) and the presenting complaint
Key investigations and results; procedures
Brief clinical course
**Medicines on discharge** — and every **change, with the reason** (started, stopped, dose changed)
Allergies
**Actions for the GP** (e.g. U&E in a week after starting ramipril; review the statin); follow-up arranged
What the patient was told; signature, grade, contact

tips: Medication changes with reasons: the GP can't ask you later.
Specific GP actions with a timeframe beat “please review”.

swabs.summary: Use the correct technique to apply sterile swabs to the nose, throat, skin and wounds; correct containers, labelling and prompt dispatch.

sections.title: Why
items: Site-specific technique + correct transport medium + prompt dispatch are what score.

sections.title: Indications
items: MRSA screening (nose/perineum)
Suspected wound infection
Sore throat / suspected strep
Viral testing (nasopharyngeal)

sections.title: Equipment
items: Sterile swab + appropriate transport medium (bacterial/viral)
Gloves; request form

sections.title: Technique by site
items: Throat: swab the tonsils/posterior pharynx, avoiding the tongue and cheeks
Nasal: insert 2–3 cm, rotate against the mucosa
Nasopharyngeal (viral): pass along the floor of the nose to the nasopharynx, rotate, hold briefly
Wound: clean first, then the **Levine technique** — press and rotate the swab over 1 cm² of viable wound bed for 5 seconds (not the slough)

sections.title: After
items: Place in the correct medium; label; send promptly (viral samples especially)

tips: Correct **site technique** is the marked point (avoid the tongue for throat swabs).
Right transport medium for the organism sought.
Label and send promptly.

dressing.summary: Provide basic care of surgical or traumatic wounds and apply dressings appropriately (includes basic suturing).

sections.title: Why
items: Assess, clean, close appropriately, dress. Suturing must be demonstrable by **either a hand-held tie or an instrument tie** in the exam.

sections.title: Indications
items: Simple lacerations, surgical wound closure/dressing

sections.title: Equipment
items: Suture pack (needle holder, toothed forceps, scissors)
Suture material (appropriate gauge)
Local anaesthetic
Cleaning/irrigation solution, dressing

sections.title: Assess & prepare
items: Examine depth, contamination, neurovascular and tendon status; check tetanus
Clean and irrigate the wound thoroughly
Infiltrate local anaesthetic and test

sections.title: Close
items: Choose the method: **sutures**, adhesive strips (Steri-Strips), tissue glue, or staples
Load the needle ~⅔ from tip to thread in the needle holder
Pierce perpendicular (**90°**) ~4 mm from the wound edge, with **equal bites and depth** either side
Evert the edges, instrument-tie the knot (~3 throws), and space sutures evenly
Aim for good apposition without tension

sections.title: After
items: Apply a dressing; give wound-care and red-flag advice (infection)
Advise suture-removal timing: face ~5 days, scalp 7–10, limbs/trunk 10–14

pairs.title: Key facts
rows: Technique: needle **90°** to skin, ~4 mm bite from the edge, equal depth either side, edges everted
Suture removal: face ~5 days · scalp 7–10 · limbs/trunk 10–14 · over joints ~14
Suture choice: **non-absorbable monofilament** (nylon/polypropylene) for skin; absorbable (e.g. Vicryl) for deep/buried layers
Do not primarily close: mammalian bites, grossly contaminated, or wounds >6–12 h old

tips: Be ready to suture by hand-held **or** instrument tie.
Don’t primarily close bites/contaminated wounds; consider tetanus.
Quote suture-removal times by body site.

scrub.summary: Follow approved processes for cleaning hands and wearing PPE before procedures or surgical operations.

sections.title: Why
items: Sterile technique for theatre. The whole point is **not to contaminate** — keep hands above the elbows and never touch anything non-sterile.

sections.title: Indications
items: Any sterile/aseptic procedure or surgical operation

sections.title: Equipment
items: Scrub sink
Antiseptic (4% chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
Sterile gown & gloves, sterile towel, nail brush/pick

sections.title: Prepare
items: Don theatre hat and mask; remove jewellery; open the sterile gown/glove pack onto a clean surface
Perform a social hand wash first

sections.title: Surgical scrub
items: Clean under the nails
Wash hands and forearms to the elbows using antiseptic, keeping **hands above the elbows** so water runs off at the elbow
Follow the timed/structured technique (per product — commonly the first scrub ~3–5 min)
Dry with a sterile towel, hands first then towards the elbow

sections.title: Gown & glove
items: Don the sterile gown without touching the outside
Use the **closed-glove** technique; keep hands within the cuffs until gloved

tips: Keep hands above elbows throughout — the classic marked point.
Never touch a non-sterile surface once scrubbed; if in doubt, re-scrub.
Closed-glove technique.

nutrition.summary: Screen with **MUST**, act on the score, and know refeeding syndrome before feeding a malnourished patient.

sections.title: MUST
items: Unplanned weight loss in 3–6 months: <5% = 0, 5–10% = 1, >10% = 2
Acutely ill with no intake for >5 days: 2
Total: 0 low, 1 medium (monitor), **2+ high (dietitian)**

sections.title: Refeeding (NICE CG32)
items: At risk: very low BMI, little intake for >5–10 days, low phosphate, potassium or magnesium before feeding
Start slowly (as low as 10 kcal/kg/day in the highest risk), thiamine before feeding, check phosphate

tips: Low phosphate is the hallmark of refeeding.

paeds-calc.summary: Estimate or use the weight, calculate per kilogram, check against the maximum, and show your working.

sections.title: Weight (APLS estimates)
items: 1–12 months: (0.5 × age in months) + 4
1–5 years: (2 × age) + 8
6–12 years: (3 × age) + 7

sections.title: Doses
items: Dose = mg/kg × weight; never exceed the adult dose; use the BNFC (often age- or weight-banded)
Concentrations: 1% = 10 mg/mL

sections.title: Fluids
items: Maintenance (NICE NG29, Holliday–Segar): 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg, 20 mL/kg/day for each kg above 20
Bolus: 10 mL/kg

tips: Write units at every step.
Sense-check the answer against the adult dose.

postnatal.summary: Advice for the weeks after birth: mood, feeding, contraception, recovery, safe sleep — and the red flags that mean come back.

sections.title: Mother
items: Mood: baby blues (days, settles), postnatal depression, puerperal psychosis (emergency)
Bleeding (lochia), perineum or wound, pelvic floor exercises
Contraception: fertility can return from about day 21

sections.title: Baby
items: Feeding support; **safe sleep**: on the back, feet to foot, no co-sleeping after alcohol, drugs or smoking

sections.title: Red flags
items: Heavy bleeding, fever, calf swelling or breathlessness, headache or visual change (pre-eclampsia can occur after birth), thoughts of harm

sections.title: Tips
items: Ask about mood directly.

formula.summary: Teach a parent to make up formula safely, step by step, then have them tell it back.

sections.title: Steps (NHS)
items: Clean surface, wash hands, sterilised bottle
Boil fresh tap water; let it cool **no more than 30 minutes** (so it's still at least 70 °C, which kills bacteria)
Water in first, then the exact number of **level** scoops (don't pack)
Shake; cool under a cold tap; test on the inside of the wrist
Use within 2 hours; throw away leftovers; make each feed fresh

sections.title: Tips
items: Ask them to show you.
Too much powder dehydrates; too little underfeeds.

cse-referral-2.summary: A letter from what you watched or read that tells the receiving team, in the first lines, **who the patient is, what you're asking, and how urgently** — then only the information they need.

sections.title: Layout
items: Your details and the recipient's (department, consultant), date
Patient name, DOB, NHS number, address
**Reason for referral** and the **urgency** (e.g. suspected cancer pathway) in the opening sentence
HPC — the relevant positives and negatives
Examination and investigation results
PMH, drugs, **allergies**, social situation that affects care
What you have already done or started, and your **specific question**
Signature, name, role, contact

tips: If the reader only reads the first two lines, they should know what you want.
Select: a referral is not a full history.
Normal values are provided — flag the abnormal ones.

cse-request.summary: Fill the request so the radiologist or lab can justify, protocol and prioritise it: the clinical question is the heart of it.

sections.title: Fields
items: Patient identifiers; location; your name, grade, bleep
The **investigation** and the body part, with urgency
**Clinical details**: the history and findings that justify it
The **question to answer** (“?pulmonary embolism”, “?free air”)
Safety: pregnancy status, renal function and allergy for contrast, metal or implants for MRI, anticoagulation for invasive tests

tips: Ask a question; don't just list symptoms.
IR(ME)R: the request must justify the radiation dose — give enough for that.
